**Vishnu KS** · 2017-06-28 16:38 UTC

I left hostel a day before and is at home which means I don't have access to high speed internet. I have been trying to do provision for a quite long time now and it fails in the middle due to internet problems.  One particular step which is collecting mypy takes lot of time and is repeated each every time even though it ran successful in the last provison attempt. Each time mypy is cloned it is downloaded to a different folder.( eg /tmp/pip-3pp4zsnt-build) Is there any reason we are downloading it each time?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-28 16:45 UTC

I'm not really sure this is relevant, but it's interesting that mypy is tied to a particular commit.  I wonder if pip is not able to cache that?  You'd think it could use the git hash.

~~~
 ~/zulip/requirements (review-5589) $ grep mypy *
mypy.txt:git+https://github.com/python/mypy.git@71efcdb29226e1dd76b2fe95982c82588807173b
py3_dev.txt:-r mypy.txt

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-28 16:47 UTC

It might be worth just commenting out the `-r mypy.txt` line in `py3_dev.txt` to try to get the rest of provision working.  I doubt mypy is really needed for anything other than running the mypy checks as part of test-all.

**Vishnu KS** · 2017-06-28 16:51 UTC

Yeah. I will try that. We should probably do something about dependencies which are collected using a commit. Would be useful for folks who are on limited/slow internet connection :)

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-28 21:30 UTC

Agreed, that seems like an unfortunate bug in pip -- it should cache by commit ID when that's how a dependency is specified. That's more dependable to cache by than a version number in the first place. :)

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-28 21:30 UTC

And we should do something to work around it, after debugging a bit to confirm that it's a pip bug and not some issue in how we're invoking it.

requirements/mypy.txt:git+https://github.com/python/mypy.git@71efcdb29226e1dd76b2fe95982c82588807173b

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-08-11 01:39 UTC

Do not run `vagrant` as root.

**Daniel Herrarte** · 2020-08-11 01:49 UTC

I tried and it showed me this message '`initialize': Permission denied @ rb_sysopen - /home/jazz/.vagrant.d/data/machine-index/index.lock (Errno::EACCES)'

**ReCore** · 2020-08-11 01:51 UTC

run this
```
sudo groupadd docker
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER
```
Log out then log back in

**ReCore** · 2020-08-11 01:52 UTC

then to test run `docker run hello-world`

**ReCore** · 2020-08-11 01:53 UTC

if you get something like this:
```
WARNING: Error loading config file: /home/user/.docker/config.json -
stat /home/user/.docker/config.json: permission denied
```
run
```
sudo chown "$USER":"$USER" /home/"$USER"/.docker -R
sudo chmod g+rwx "$HOME/.docker" -R
```

**ReCore** · 2020-08-11 01:54 UTC

Again log out then back in

**ReCore** · 2020-08-11 01:56 UTC

it creates a group with root access, adds you to it then adds docker to it, giving you both the same permission levels when using docker. The second command set just makes sure docker has root powers

**Daniel Herrarte** · 2020-08-11 02:06 UTC

Thank you a lot @ReCore ,  I'm going to work on this tomorrow

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-08-11 02:14 UTC

I would not recommend editing any permission bits (`chmod g+rwx`). The default permissions are correct.

And if you’re following our [documentation](https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/development/setup-vagrant.html#ubuntu), you’ll already have added yourself to the `docker` group by this point.

Running `vagrant` as root has created files owned by root in your home directory that prevent you from running `vagrant` normally. I expect you’ll just need to run `sudo chown -R "$USER:" ~/.vagrant.d/`, and maybe do the same with other files in your home directory depending on what problems you run into.

**Andrea  Longo** · 2016-09-27 14:50 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-09-27 16:40 UTC

@Andrea Longo the story here is that `run-dev.py` runs on port 9991 and is a proxy to other services running on ports 9992 through 9994.  Those other services include third-party code that prints out when they have finished starting up what ports they are on.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-09-27 16:41 UTC

So, that's why we have this somewhat confusing situation

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-09-27 16:41 UTC

I think it'd be better to fix the confusing situation in some way, since you're not the only person who's been tripped up by that "port 9992" message

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-09-27 16:42 UTC

One approach would be to also print out something from the proxy code explaining what's going on

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-09-27 16:42 UTC

e.g. "Starting proxy on port 9991 and services on 9992-9994.  Note that in the Zulip Vagrant environment, only port 9991 is exposed to the host machine"

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-09-27 16:43 UTC

Fixing this in a way you like could be a great first contribution.

**Andrea  Longo** · 2016-09-27 16:57 UTC

@Tim Abbott I had the same thought, that messaging is one of the bugs I was planning to open. We certainly went through plenty of iterations of startup messaging with a previous product I worked on, dev would think "oh yeah obvs" and customers would be "huh?"

Btw, for a more verbose version of my first install experience, I just finished a blog post here: http://www.feorlen.org/2016/09/27/playing-with-zulip/

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-09-27 17:03 UTC

Cool re: blog post.  I'd love to patch some of the documentation holes that you noticed while working on this; while we've tried hard to make it comprehensive (overall developer documentation passed 50k words recently), it's surprisingly challenging to determine everything that needs to be covered.

**Andrea  Longo** · 2016-09-27 17:11 UTC

Users will always be coming up with something unexpected, and almost always there is a seemingly (to the user) rational reason. 

Sometimes people give me grief about "non-standard" habits (disabling JS, changing font sizes, languages, and keyboards, self-hosting) but I'm always finding weird little bugs as a result. If I need a pristine environment, I know where to find one. I try to write things up as much as I can when I know it will be cheerfully accepted.

**Andrea  Longo** · 2016-09-27 17:12 UTC

Oh, and in case it's not obvious, I'm no stranger to writing docs :)

**Andrea  Longo** · 2016-09-29 16:27 UTC

I wanted to note a problem I had with my Ubuntu 14.04 machine, which isn't caused by Zulip but starting up the server processes and getting incoming connections triggered it. And by "it" I mean "the wireless interface falling over." The short answer is "something something wpa_supplicant #*!@ systemd" according to my resident network admin. 


When my dhcp lease expired (which maybe should not have happened) wpa_supplicant became unhappy about the existing static network configuration and charged in to save the day in the name of dynamic address allocation. There was an epic battle, and in the resulting fray the wireless interface suffered a fatal blow. This is something of a problem for an already headless box.


The money quote in this conversation: "You can blame systemd if you want. That would make me happy." 


I have a bit of a unique configuration for a server, wireless rather than ethernet, but it's otherwise a stock Ubuntu install. Perhaps this will save someone else from several hours of headache.

**Sumana Harihareswara** · 2016-11-04 15:03 UTC

So @Aswin kumar: Right now we do not have a feature that allows anyone to really properly move a conversation from one stream to another; when I mean "properly" I mean, "take the whole conversation and replace all its metadata". There also is not an easy way for a user to indicate "**this** conversation is a continuation of **that** conversation" without manually posting links in both topics, each pointing to the other topic. I would like that feature: display two streams/narrows as linked to each other. https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/1366 is an open issue for that; if someone fixes it, I'll have my wish. :) 

So what I did was more social than technical: I said, in plain English prose, "I want to move over there", and then clicked on the stream I wanted us to be talking in, and composed a new message and mentioned you.

**Sumana Harihareswara** · 2016-11-04 15:03 UTC

if options.interface is None:

**Arpith Siromoney** · 2016-10-09 15:41 UTC

basically, POST a form to /api/v1/fetch_api_key with the username and password:
```js
      const url = `${config.apiURL}/fetch_api_key`;
      const form = new FormData();
      form.append('username', config.username);
      form.append('password', config.password);
      fetch(url, {
        method: 'POST',
        body: form,
      }).then(res => res.json());
```

**Sumana Harihareswara** · 2016-10-11 15:57 UTC

I'm writing my first bash script in a super long time and running into difficulties.

I want to be able to run a single script to update several git repositories.

~~~
#!/bin/bash

# update a bunch of Zulip git repositories

checkout_repo(){ git checkout master ; git pull upstream master ; git push origin master ; git checkout - ;};

for repo in zulip zulip-android zulip-electron zulip-ios zulip.github.io;
do
    pushd ${repo};
    checkout_repo();
    popd;
done

~~~

Error:

~~~
$ ./update-zulip-repositories.sh 
./update-zulip-repositories.sh: line 10: syntax error near unexpected token `;'
./update-zulip-repositories.sh: line 10: `    checkout_repo();'
~~~

I've tried adding and removing semicolons, and that doesn't seem to help; as I mess around with that I get `end of file unexpected (expecting "}")` or `syntax error near unexpected token `popd'`. Ideas?

**Sumana Harihareswara** · 2016-10-11 15:58 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-11 16:04 UTC

So, you only need semicolons if you're putting multiple commands on the same line; so none of the lines in your for loop should have them.

Current code:

for repo in zulip zulip-android zulip-electron zulip-ios zulip.github.io

Yes

I think you need a newline or ; before `}`

**Sumana Harihareswara** · 2016-10-11 16:11 UTC

**Reid Barton** · 2016-10-11 16:11 UTC

Function definitions are super confusing...

**Reid Barton** · 2016-10-11 16:11 UTC

Normally I put a newline after the `{`, and before the `}`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-11 16:13 UTC

In general, I recommend laying out your shell script code the way you would something in another language, i.e. writing your function more like this:
```
checkout_repo() { 
    git checkout master
    git pull upstream master
    git push origin master
   git checkout - 
}
```

since the result is a lot more readable :)

There are certain words that Python treats as special magic words.

~~~.py
>>> a = blah
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
NameError: name 'blah' is not defined
>>> a = int
>>> a
<type 'int'>
~~~

So when I say `a = int` what I'm doing is I'm saying that a *is* the concept of an integer.

**Sumana Harihareswara** · 2016-10-16 21:41 UTC

~~~.py
>>> isinstance(4,a)
True
>>> isinstance(4,int)
True
~~~

**Sumana Harihareswara** · 2016-10-16 21:42 UTC

What does it mean, and how do I fix it?

I resolved the conflicting files, but when I tried to force push the fixed branch it said I needed to resolve fast-forward errors. Woah, that error is weird.  Usually a git error at the start means that you force-pushed and the tests can't find the old commits in the Git repo

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-26 23:09 UTC

> then remote origin still wouldn't accept my changes
Did you try using `git push -f`?

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-26 23:09 UTC

After rebasing, you need to force-push to any remote repository to send your changes there

**Christie Koehler** · 2016-10-26 23:14 UTC

@Laura Hampton That looks like a link to an error on  your prior pull request, not the current one

## i18n capitalization

*2016-10-30 to 2016-10-30 · 5 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/49-development-help/topic/i18n.20capitalization/with/47506)*

**Rishi Gupta** · 2016-10-30 03:55 UTC

Is there a way to do automatic capitalization for translated sentences (either python or javascript)? In particular, I have something of the form:
`_("%(foo)s must be at least 3 characters long")`
where foo is `_("Short name")` or `_("Subdomain")` depending on various settings. 

Doing a string replacement as above won't work, because there might be a language that has word order "3 characters %(foo)s must be", and now there is a weird capitalized foo in the middle of the translated sentence. So I what I really want is something like 
`_.capitalize_as_sentence(_("%(foo)s must be at least 3 characters long"))`, where foo is `_("short name")` or `_("subdomain")`.

Does that make sense? Is this possible, or should I just make two separate strings to be translated?

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-30 05:15 UTC

We have a "translation" stream that you might want to cross-post to.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-30 05:19 UTC

The pragmatic solution here is probably to just have your code dispatch to N different strings, unless `foo` is completely dynamic.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-30 05:21 UTC

And if foo is completely dynamic, say something like this: `_("Item should be at least 3 characters long:") + '  ' + foo)`

**Rishi Gupta** · 2016-10-30 06:10 UTC

good idea for the cross post, thanks! and yeah, the pragmatic solution seems like the front runner so far.


## Mypy not recognizing argparse?

*2016-11-01 to 2016-11-01 · 5 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/49-development-help/topic/Mypy.20not.20recognizing.20argparse.3F/with/48086)*

**Laura Hampton** · 2016-11-01 21:20 UTC

I seem to be running into another issue with mypy.  I updated two command files to use argparse instead of optparse, and when I ran the mypy tests on them I got the following error:
```
zerver/management/commands/create_realm.py: note: In function "add_arguments":
zerver/management/commands/create_realm.py:23: error: Name 'argparse' is not defined
```
My type annotation is this (the same as the other type annotations that worked on previous versions):
```
# type: (argparse.ArgumentParser) -> None 
```
This is one of the class methods it complains about: 
```
    def add_arguments(self, parser):
        # type: (argparse.ArgumentParser) -> None
        parser.add_argument('-d', '--domain',
                    dest='domain',
                    type=str,
                    help='The name of the realm in which you are adding people to streams.')
```
ArgumentParser is explicitly imported at the top of the file. 
I did a bit of googling and found something about Mypy not recognizing the PYTHONPATH - but I didn't want to go mucking about with that before asking my question. There is no name error if I run the scripts I changed. 
Thank you very much for your help.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-01 21:21 UTC

the issue here is that if you do `import argparse`, then you'd reference it as `argparse.ArgumentParser`

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-01 21:21 UTC

But if you do `from argparse import ArgumentParser`, you reference it as just `ArgumentParser`

**Laura Hampton** · 2016-11-01 21:29 UTC

Thank you, I adjusted those things and it fixed it. :) 
For future reference, is it best to say "from argparse import ArgumentParser" or to just import argparse?

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-01 21:31 UTC

I think for this either way is fine.  As a project we generally prefer the `from` style for our imports, so probably defaulting to that is good.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-03 20:25 UTC

Ooh I know this one!

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-03 20:26 UTC

It's probably because you have 2 auth decorators being used or something

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-03 20:27 UTC

Oh, actually, I have a better theory

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-03 20:27 UTC

So this is a thing about positional vs. keyword arguments in Python

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-03 20:27 UTC

If you pass more positional arguments than a function takes, Python will just use the extra positional arguments are the kwargs in that position

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-03 20:28 UTC

And the Zulip auth decorators cause every authed view to get two positional argument: (request, user_profile)

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-03 20:28 UTC

You're accepting the first but not the second

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-03 20:28 UTC

Of course, in your case, the second thing isn't a UserProfile, it's a RemoteServer or whatever, but the principle is the same

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-03 20:29 UTC

@Lisa Neigut FYI

**Lisa Neigut** · 2016-11-03 20:29 UTC

oh interesting

**Lisa Neigut** · 2016-11-03 20:30 UTC

if i understand correctly, the issue is that i need to add a 2nd positional argument for the 'user_profile' to my decorated method?

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-03 20:31 UTC

yep!

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-03 20:32 UTC

A good technique for debugging that particular class of exception is to make the function just accept `(*args, **kwargs)` and then print those out to see what's being passed in.

**Lisa Neigut** · 2016-11-03 20:42 UTC

@Aswin kumar Another way to ask the question you asked is: how do we prevent regressions? A regression is a newly introduced bug that breaks existing functionality. And we work hard to prevent regressions -- a huge part of that is our automated test suite. We aim to make it possible for you, a new contributor, to write improvements to Zulip and to use the existing automated tests to verify that you have not introduced any regressions. And, to pass along that same guarantee to future developers, you also have to include tests with new features or bugfixes that you submit.

## removing extraneous files from commit

*2016-11-06 to 2016-11-08 · 14 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/49-development-help/topic/removing.20extraneous.20files.20from.20commit/with/49777)*

**Shashank** · 2016-11-06 08:25 UTC

I have added some extraneous files in my commit , could some one tell me on how to remove those files and commit the changes again.

**Reyha Verma** · 2016-11-06 09:08 UTC

@Shashank  You can do ``git reflog`` . You will see a log of all the git operations that you have done till now. After that, you can then do ``git reset --hard <commit>`` where <commit> is the commit hash that you want to roll back to. Once you have rolled back, you can simply commit the changes again.

**Shashank** · 2016-11-06 10:51 UTC

Can I push the changes to new branch and compare the changes with new branch.

**Vishnu KS** · 2016-11-06 10:54 UTC

Why not push the changes to the same branch?

**Vishnu KS** · 2016-11-06 11:03 UTC

@Shashank Are you facing any trouble pushing to the same branch?

**Shashank** · 2016-11-06 12:28 UTC

Yes @Vishnu Ks  I am facing some problems. Actually I committed some unnecessary files and unable to remove them from pull request and push the changes to that branch.

**Aakash Tyagi** · 2016-11-06 15:22 UTC

@Shashank you should try rebasing to remove the files from the last commit. Here is how you an do that.
* Start rebasing.
```
git rebase -i HEAD~2 (This will prompt you to choose the commit (from last 2 commits) you want to edit)
```

* Write `edit` in front of the commit  you'd want to edit.

* Now, you can remove the file from that commit using the command :
```
git rm --cached file_name
```

* After removing all the files, you can continue the rebase.
```
git rebase --continue
```

* Then you can force push to the branch you are working on.

Hope this helps! You can learn more about rebasing via this [resource](https://www.atlassian.com/git/tutorials/rewriting-history/git-rebase-i).

**Vishnu KS** · 2016-11-06 16:11 UTC

@Shashank The thing you have to keep in mind is that whatever changes you make to the branch would automatically appear in the PR. Once you have corrected the commit in your local copy using git reset or any other method  update the branch using `git push remote-name branch-name --force`. This would replace the remote branch with the same copy as your system. Always take extra care when you use force update as it replaces the remote branch completely with a local version. It may lead to loss of history.

## Custom chat server

*2016-11-08 to 2016-11-09 · 8 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/49-development-help/topic/Custom.20chat.20server/with/50783)*

**Richard Prosser** · 2016-11-08 20:51 UTC

Hi, I am hoping to use Zulip to implement an online wargame service, whereby messages from players may be deliberately delayed (in game time) or even mangled 'en route' by umpires, who I presume would be Realm Administrators. This means that all messages from players would have to be routed via the umpires, with a scheduler (queue) sending them onwards later.

I've had a look at the documentation - which seems extensive - but I don't quite see where/what I need to modify. I don't think that this is a Webhook arrangement for example, more like a new branch of the code. I am familiar with Python so I should be able to write the new stuff without much difficulty.

Also I am reluctant to produce my own clients though I acknowledge that I may have to. I may restrict myself to providing  a web-based client and simply using the others (Android, for example) to receive the delayed messages in the usual manner.

I would welcome any suggestions as to how I should proceed, bearing in mind that I wll no doubt want to integrate any core updates as and when they occur.


Thanks ...

Richard

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-08 21:00 UTC

Hi @Richard Prosser!  You'll need to fork the code to do this, but it probably won't be that hard.  Basically, you'll want to change the something above `do_send_messages` in the code path to put messages in your approval queue, and then actually call `do_send_messages` once the send is approved by the umpires

**Steve Howell** · 2016-11-08 21:00 UTC

Using Zulip as a gaming platform is a neat idea, and it may require some cleverness to adapt it.  One thing you might want to study for a little bit is some of our webhook integrations, because those are examples where we take incoming messages and process them in the server.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-11-08 21:02 UTC

I would try to hack up something simple like tic-tac-toe first, and see if we can merge a really simple gaming engine like that.

**Richard Prosser** · 2016-11-09 13:55 UTC

Thanks for the replies. I am now wondering if there should be 'hooks' to call some custom code, if it exists. What do you think?

**Steve Howell** · 2016-11-09 14:38 UTC

We are trying to move toward having some custom apps run inside the Zulip server.  Basically, the idea is that you can write things like a game server with a bot that mediates everything, but then you're paying all the latency hops, so we'd want to take certain user-contributed bots and make them runnable on the server (w/the admin turning them on or off).  You can see some details here:

http://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/custom-apps.html

**Steve Howell** · 2016-11-09 14:39 UTC

In principle, there's no real architectural restriction on having some custom code run on the server--we just haven't built it out yet.  (We'd need the custom pieces to be reasonably efficient.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-09 18:38 UTC

More relevant for @Richard Prosser's application is that we don't have an existing mechanism to put hooks to delay or block sending of messages; it would be easy to build though, e.g. by intercepting the `message_sender` RabbitMQ queue.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-11-11 06:24 UTC

```
 12 function filter_streams_by_search(streams) {
 13     var search_box = $(".stream-list-filter");
 14 
 15     var search_term = search_box.expectOne().val().trim();
 16 
 17     if (search_term === '') {
 18         return streams;
 19     }
 20 
 21     var search_terms = search_term.toLowerCase().split(",");
 22     search_terms = _.map(search_terms, function (s) {
 23         return s.trim();
 24     });
 25 
 26     var filtered_streams = _.filter(streams, function (stream) {
 27         return _.any(search_terms, function (search_term) {
 28             var lower_stream_name = stream.toLowerCase().split(" ");
 29             return _.any(lower_stream_name, function (name) {
 30                 return name.indexOf(search_term) === 0;
 31             });
 32         });  
 33     });      
 34 
 35     return filtered_streams;
```

```
if options.interface is None:
    user_id = os.getuid()
    user_name = pwd.getpwuid(user_id).pw_name
    if user_name == "vagrant":
        # In the Vagrant development environment, we need to listen on
        # all ports, and it's safe to do so, because Vagrant is only
        # exposing certain guest ports (by default just 9991) to the host.
        options.interface = ""
    else:
        # Otherwise, only listen to requests on localhost for security.
        options.interface = "127.0.0.1"
```

**Dennis Payonk** · 2016-11-22 21:28 UTC

would changing the hostname of the machine potentially cause connectivity problems?

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-22 21:31 UTC

It would break rabbitmq (rabbitmq, amazingly, keys its database to the hostname; we're planning to work around that in the next release by pinning it to use localhost as the hostname for that purpose by default).

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-22 21:32 UTC

One solution is to purge rabbitmq, run `scripts/setup/configure-rabbitmq`, and then restart the server

**Dennis Payonk** · 2016-11-22 21:34 UTC

thanks...should i have been able to google that, or look in GH issues for that?  I hate to bother with install issues if i can self service

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-22 21:35 UTC

there's several googlable GitHub issues documenting that workaround

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-22 21:35 UTC

but the hope is to eliminate it -- it's by far the top production install issue.

**Dennis Payonk** · 2016-11-22 21:46 UTC

thx...there should be a https://lmgtfy.com/?q=rabbitmq+zulip bot for some of this stuff

**Kevin Riggle** · 2016-11-23 03:24 UTC

what's worse is that behavior is not RabbitMQ's fault but due to an underlying Erlang design decision.

`var before_punctuation = '\\s|^|>|[\\(\\".,\';\\[]';` `var after_punctuation = '\\s|$|<|[\\)\\"\\?!:.,\';\\]!]';` please help me understand what these regular expressions are doing

**Prafful Javare** · 2019-04-02 16:10 UTC

brickbite says in the comment that we should just ignore the content inside a span tag, how can I proceed to do that? Also what does ignore actually mean?

**Steve Howell** · 2019-04-02 16:21 UTC

@Prafful Javare Here are things that are allowed to come before the regex:

* `\s` - whitespace
* `^` - start of line
* `>".,';[` - punctuation

There's a lot of escaping that has to happen.  I would read up on regexes (via google) to understand this code better.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-04-02 16:23 UTC

I hope it goes without saying that this is a pretty ambitious change.  We would essentially need to write a custom parser to go through the message.  And it's not necessarily going to be faster than the regex approach.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-04-02 16:25 UTC

Somehow this had a "good first issue" tag on it.  I removed that tag.  This is definitely non-trivial.  The only thing that's easy about it is that all the complexity would be in just the one function, and it's pretty easy to rigorously unit test parsing code.  But the internals are gonna be tricky.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-04-02 16:32 UTC

A good warmup here would be to write a function that simply finds all the words (and offsets) in a message.  And the definition of a word is basically anything surrounded by spaces or certain punctuation characters.  Plus the boundary conditions of the first and last words.

**Akash Kothawale** · 2017-03-23 07:21 UTC

Apart from `--strict-optional` support, is there are anything else that needs to be done to make type checking more powerful? 

I was making a GSOC proposal draft for this and thought I should discuss its scope.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-23 13:34 UTC

@Akash Kothawale I can give you a couple ideas...

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-23 13:38 UTC

One thing is that we should probably write a tool  that audits our code for really long or repetitive mypy declarations.  A mypy declaration that says `(bool, bool, bool, bool, bool, bool, bool, bool,  str, bool) -> None` is kind of useless to catch the main class of bug, which is putting bool parameters in the wrong order.  So we might end up refactoring code or figuring out a way to introduce stronger mypy types.  Similarly, some functions may have really complicated data structures being pass in, so you'll see stuff like `List[Dict[str, Union[str, Tuple[str, int]]]` that kind of make your head explode, and for those, we'll want to either figure out how to simplify the code or how to extract custom mypy types.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-23 13:41 UTC

Then, a more experimental idea would be to try to better integrate our own custom dynamic type-checking system with mypy.  If you look at `zerver/lib/validator.py`, you'll see that we have a composable way of building type checkers that run at runtime.  It may be possible to have those things somehow code-generate mypy statements or even mypy  stubs.  And then we could have some kind of tooling that makes sure the mypy static declarations for functions are consistent with the run-time validators.  I'm being kind of hand-way here, because I don't have a vision for exactly how this would work, but I'm confident there's some pretty nice way to do this.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-23 13:44 UTC

Also, any student who works on mypy this summer will probably have some "grunt work" to do, but it's highly appreciated grunt work.  For example, we still use `Any` in many places, and we may want to sweep our code for those, and either fix the mypy declarations (i.e. where the original person was either just lax  or working with an older version of mypy) or figure out better ways to structure the code so that stricter static typing can happen.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-23 18:15 UTC

For the `(bool, bool, bool, bool, bool, bool, bool, bool,  str, bool) -> None`, there's actually a different syntax supported that doesn't have this problem; we use it in exactly one place (`generic_bulk_cached_fetch`) but could use it in more.

The other relevant note is that if we desupport Python 2, we can use the nicer Python 3 style syntax

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-23 18:15 UTC

Also, adding some sort of typeshed stubs for Django would make a lot more type-checking possible, since we make heavy use of the dependency

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-12-03 19:43 UTC

I assume you're using Windows?

**Robert Hönig** · 2016-12-03 19:43 UTC

Unfortunately, yes.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-12-03 19:43 UTC

OK so here's your problem; windows messes up line-feeds, and so we have git configured to auto-fix that, with excludes for some file types:
```
$ cat .gitattributes 
*   text=auto eol=lf
*.gif binary
*.jpg binary
*.eot binary
*.woff binary
*.svg binary
*.ttf binary
*.png binary
*.otf binary
*.tif binary
.gitignore export-ignore
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-12-03 19:44 UTC

I think the conclusion is you should be naming your file `.png`, not `.PNG`, and then it'll stop doing this.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-12-03 19:44 UTC

(We use lower-case names for extensions in general anyway)

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-10 18:18 UTC

The rationale behind asking for your password is that if your computer is not secure, somebody can steal your API key. I'm wondering if we can think of something shorter that describes this clearly; any ideas?

`show_PMs_in_notifications` maybe?

Ok.

Its friends all have long names, e.g. `page_params.enable_offline_push_notifications` so it doesn't need to be short, just not ultra-long :)

`notify_private_messages` maybe?

Ah ok

## Digital Ocean and Pull Requests

*2016-12-17 to 2017-01-12 · 5 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/49-development-help/topic/Digital.20Ocean.20and.20Pull.20Requests/with/96136)*

**Arpith Siromoney** · 2016-12-17 15:58 UTC

Now that we have a script to generate droplets, it might be cool to create a droplet when a PR is made for the main zulip repo. This could help with code review/testing. Thoughts? Comments? :pizza: ?

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-17 16:02 UTC

I think we get Digital Ocean stuff discounted or free for GCI, but I assume that for your proposal we'd have to pay for it, so I'm not sure the economics would work out well.  I think realistically most of the time I test somebody's PR, I simply fetch it and run it in my environment.  This allows me to use my native editor setup if I want to change the code around a bit or add debugging statements.

**Arpith Siromoney** · 2016-12-17 16:09 UTC

Ah, yeah 5 * 120 might be a bit much, I assumed the discount/free was because we were open source (not GCI)

**Sumana Harihareswara** · 2017-01-12 14:53 UTC

@Arpith Siromoney We were motivated to get this going because of GCI, and the fact that GCI is about open source reallllly helps - @Christie Koehler was able to get the sponsorship from DigitalOcean because they're particularly excited that GCI is a project introducing pre-university students to open source development. I think they wouldn't necessarily do this for any arbitrary "get kids coding" initiative.

**Sumana Harihareswara** · 2017-01-12 14:55 UTC

@Arpith Siromoney if you & other potential reviewers are slowed down in reviewing and testing by the friction of spinning up a dev env that includes the PR, then maybe we could talk about something that's like what you thought about, and is easy to kick off but not 100% automatic and that runs on Kandra Labs's money (which means we would gatekeep who has the privileges to do it).

Hi, 
In the stream search logic inside static/js/subs.js, are the streams having some part of their name matched with the last search term being displayed ? If so, why are the names matched only with the last search term? (The search terms are being formed here by splitting the search query by ',' character )
```
flag = flag && (function () {
            var sub_name = sub.name.toLowerCase();
            var matches_list = search_terms.indexOf(sub_name) > -1;
            var matches_last_val = sub_name.match(search_terms[search_terms.length - 1]);

            return matches_list || matches_last_val;
}());
```

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-19 15:13 UTC

@Brock Whittaker Can you look into that?  ^^

**Brock Whittaker** · 2016-12-20 00:07 UTC

Not totally sure what the bug you are seeing is.

For example when I type in `announce` I get only `announce`. By typing in `announce, ` I get everything again, but if I then type in `announce, ba`, I get `announce` and `backend`.

It only fully matches things before the last comma and then will partial match everything after the last comma.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-20 00:27 UTC

Is the idea that you're expecting people to keep typing "ba" to "backend"?  If that's the case, I think we should add some comments in the code to explain the semantics.  I would also think that "ann, ba" should still match announce.

**Brock Whittaker** · 2016-12-20 00:31 UTC

That definitely makes sense as a process for matching as well, it just wasn't the original filtering method. However I think it'd be a good change. What do you think @Tim Abbott?

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-20 01:09 UTC

I think we've had 15 variations of these types of searches floating around our codebase at one point.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-20 01:09 UTC

There should be an implementation for the left sidebar filter.  I think the first step is to make subs.js consistent with that by reusing the same code.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-20 01:10 UTC

Then once both of our stream filters go through the same code, we can refine the search semantics as we go forward.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-20 01:13 UTC

Yeah, see filter_streams_by_search() in stream_list.js.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-20 01:14 UTC

It would be nice to put some node tests on this code, too, like we do for some of the people-searching code.

**Vaibhav Singhal** · 2016-12-20 18:01 UTC

## eslint no-undef

*2016-12-20 to 2016-12-21 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/49-development-help/topic/eslint.20no-undef/with/100025)*

**Rishi Gupta** · 2016-12-20 22:43 UTC

What is a good way to handle the eslint no-undef rule for things included from dependencies? In particular, I'm trying to use Plotly functions from plotly.js. I've added plotly.js to the package.json dependencies, and have gotten things to work in the browser, but am getting eslint errors like
```
  42:5  error  'Plotly' is not defined                                           no-undef
```
(I guess relatedly, why isn't the linter giving errors for things from jquery or i18next or the other javascript dependencies? Does Plotly need to be added to some sort of exclude list?)

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-20 23:29 UTC

There's a big globals section in the config file:

```
 ~/zulip (master *) $ cat .eslintrc.json 
{
    "env": {
        "node": true
    },
    "globals": {
        "$": false,
        "_": false,
        "jQuery": false,
        "Spinner": false,
        "Handlebars": false,

**Rishi Gupta** · 2016-12-21 00:12 UTC

awesome, thanks!

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-12-21 15:32 UTC

I wonder if we should try to rewrite that error message to mention something about the need to declare the global.

**Sampriti Panda** · 2016-12-22 12:54 UTC

So as a part of this issue (in the topic), I need to write a validator/converter which will take the user_profile as an argument.

**Sampriti Panda** · 2016-12-22 12:54 UTC

Now since user_profile itself is another argument, I can't directly pass it/

**Sampriti Panda** · 2016-12-22 12:54 UTC

So, I was thinking of passing it as a string and then resolving it in has_request_variables.

**Sampriti Panda** · 2016-12-22 12:54 UTC

but that doesn't seem very "clean"

**Sampriti Panda** · 2016-12-22 12:54 UTC

any other ideas?

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-12-22 14:23 UTC

hmm

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-12-22 14:24 UTC

@Sampriti Panda it's possible we should just abandon this idea as not that useful

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-12-22 14:24 UTC

I hadn't thought about needing the `user_profile` object as an argument

**Sampriti Panda** · 2016-12-22 14:41 UTC

If it was any other variable, it wouldn't have been that difficult

**Sampriti Panda** · 2016-12-22 14:42 UTC

There is no other way to access user_profile?

**Sampriti Panda** · 2016-12-22 14:42 UTC

Like from some function.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-12-22 14:45 UTC

well

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-12-22 14:45 UTC

I think if we made a new type of REQ item

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-12-22 14:45 UTC

one could access it

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-12-22 14:45 UTC

Basically, `has_request_variables` is always being used in a context where an auth decorator is passing in the user_profile object as the second argument

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-12-22 14:45 UTC

(positional argument)

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-12-22 14:45 UTC

but it doesn't pass that on to the converter

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-22 14:51 UTC

My two cents here is that when you start validating multiple parameters against each other, it may make sense to have a nice helper function (which we already do in this case), but I would **not** incorporate that into our decorator mechanism.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-12-22 14:52 UTC

well, it's technically one parameter against the current user, which feels a bit different

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-22 14:54 UTC

Yeah, that's fair.   This is obviously a subjective decision, so I'm just giving my opinion here, but I like the way the code reads now.  Decorators have some convenience, but I also like explicit validation right in the body of the function for some sorts of things, too.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-12-22 15:02 UTC

yeah, mostly I just want it to be the case that we can ban doing a direct lookup without that method; we should possibly just change this task into a lint rule for not `Message.objects.get()` in view files

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-22 15:08 UTC

One way to help enforce this would be to use a really small class that wraps access_message and Message.objects.get() with two methods: validate() and get().  The only state that the class would manage is not allowing you to call get() if you haven't validated.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-22 15:09 UTC

some thing like `class MessageGetter(object)`

**Sampriti Panda** · 2016-12-22 15:32 UTC

> we can ban doing a direct lookup without that method;

Can you explain this?

We aren't doing this now, are we?

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-22 15:35 UTC

Not yet.

**Sampriti Panda** · 2016-12-22 15:46 UTC

So, what do you suggest I do?

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-22 15:48 UTC

We need to wait for @Tim Abbott to decide.  But I'd be inclined to abandon this for now.  My two cents is that we have some more pressing issues, and based on what I've seen from your other commits, you are probably able to tackle some of our tougher problems. :)

**Sampriti Panda** · 2016-12-22 15:58 UTC

Haha, thanks!
Any issue you would recommend?

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-22 16:03 UTC

Not off the top of my head.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-12-22 17:24 UTC

yeah, I agree, let's abandon this one

**Sampriti Panda** · 2016-12-22 17:33 UTC

I've abandoned the task.

**Sampriti Panda** · 2016-12-22 17:33 UTC

Is there a way to delete tasks in your interface?

**Steve Howell** · 2016-12-22 19:15 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-13 21:34 UTC

@Greg Price In case you're wondering what `vagrant provision` does differently than running `./tools/provision` inside the box (I prefer the latter), here is the relevant code from `Vagrantfile`:

~~~ sh
$provision_script = <<SCRIPT
set -x
set -e
set -o pipefail
# If the host is running SELinux remount the /sys/fs/selinux directory as read only,
# needed for apt-get to work.
if [ -d "/sys/fs/selinux" ]; then
  sudo mount -o remount,ro /sys/fs/selinux
fi

# Set default locale, this prevents errors if the user has another locale set.
if ! grep -q 'LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8' /etc/default/locale; then
    echo "LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8" | sudo tee -a /etc/default/locale
fi

# Provision the development environment
ln -nsf /srv/zulip ~/zulip
/srv/zulip/tools/provision

# Run any custom provision hooks the user has configured
if [ -f /srv/zulip/tools/custom_provision ]; then
  chmod +x /srv/zulip/tools/custom_provision
  /srv/zulip/tools/custom_provision
fi
SCRIPT

~~~

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-13 21:35 UTC

If you live in the US, don't run SELinux, and don't have custom provision scripts you like to run, then the two options are basically equivalent.

**Sampriti Panda** · 2016-12-31 00:02 UTC

Can you tell me how?

**Thomas de Mol** · 2016-12-31 00:04 UTC

activate takes 2 arguments, raw_operators and opts. `raw_operators` will be an array that looks like this: `[{operand: <streamname>, operator: "stream"}, {operand: <topicname>, operator: "topic"}]` And <streamname> and <topicname> would be the name of the stream and topic.

And what i used for opts was `{select_fist_unread: true, trigger: "notification click"}` (I made it for when people clicked notifications, so you should change it accordingly)

```
import json
from collections import OrderedDict

emo_file = open("emoji_map.json", 'r')

emoji_map = OrderedDict(sorted(json.load(emo_file).items()))

emo_file.close()

emo_list = []

majordict = OrderedDict([])


for key, value in emoji_map.items():
	if value not in emo_list:
		emo_list.append(value)
		majordict.setdefault(key,value)



emo_file = open("TRY.json", 'w')

final_file = open("major.json",'w')

json.dump(majordict,final_file, indent=4, sort_keys=True)

json.dump(emoji_map,emo_file, indent=4, sort_keys=True)

```

## PR workflow and process

*2017-01-06 to 2017-01-11 · 26 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/49-development-help/topic/PR.20workflow.20and.20process/with/117694)*

**Andrea  Longo** · 2017-01-06 18:56 UTC

I'd like to have a conversation about the pull request workflow and the path from "I have this thing I'm working on" to getting something merged and finalized. I realized that I wasn't really familiar with Zulip expectations around this beyond the git commands.

**Andrea  Longo** · 2017-01-06 18:57 UTC

There's a basic discussion on the mechanics of PRs in the Git guide, but it doesn't talk about the people part of the process. Some projects have little discussion on PRs, or don't encourage them unless a change is entirely complete, so historically there's a range of workflows people might be accustomed to.

**Andrea  Longo** · 2017-01-06 18:57 UTC

For Zulip, what is the expected workflow for a new PR? Many times I've seen someone request a WIP PR to investigate an issue already under discussion elsewhere. But if you have been working on something and now are ready for feedback, whether interim or nearing completion, what is the best way to go about that? Who are good people to ask, and at what stage in implementation of a new change is feedback generally anticipated?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-06 19:01 UTC

To be honest, I think it depends on the change.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-06 19:01 UTC

Our current workflow doesn't make use of much automation (I think it'd be interesting to talk about how we can use a GitHub bot automatically managing labels to make the project run more efficiently)

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-06 19:02 UTC

So the present model is this:

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-06 19:02 UTC

* If you open a PR without a WIP tag, that's a request for someone to review and potentially merge your PR

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-06 19:03 UTC

* If you open a PR with a WIP, that's a PR that you don't want to be reviewed and merged, and by default maintainers may not pay attention to it until asked for feedback explicitly (usually in the form of a comment).  (They may stop by to do a quick look and/or post a quick comment)

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-06 19:04 UTC

* Additionally, if you @-mention someone to ask for feedback, folks will provide feedback.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-06 19:05 UTC

That's basically the GitHub workflow.  Posting in chat.zulip.org is a good way to get quick immediate feedback on things

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-06 19:05 UTC

Ideally, I'd like to have a GitHub workflow that made it easier for folks to get peer review for another developer, which in general can be provided more quickly than me looking at something

**Andrea  Longo** · 2017-01-06 19:07 UTC

What got me confused was the difference between "Why don't you open a WIP so we can take a look?" and "WIP- under construction, beware falling rocks" of something that is still in progress without a specific request for feedback

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-06 19:09 UTC

Right, so in general it's very hard to help someone debug without seeing their code; so the "Create a WIP PR so we can take a look" request is asking you to create a PR (so that it's easy to look at for whoever you're talking to) while not adding it to the "things to be merged" review queue

**Andrea  Longo** · 2017-01-06 19:09 UTC

In my situation, I had a thing that was at an interim completion point, but I wasn't blocked on anything. Feedback wasn't immediately urgent, and I knew there were more pressing things (the post-holiday backlog, for example.)

**Andrea  Longo** · 2017-01-06 19:11 UTC

I had no problem with it sitting around if there was an "eventually" part of the usual workflow. When it got closer to actually blocking productive work, then I explicitly requested. Sometimes it's hard to tell the situations @-mentioning someone is part of the process or an annoying interruption.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-06 19:12 UTC

I'd say @-mentioning someone on GitHub is like emailing them; a request for something to happen eventually.  @-mentioning on chat is more of an immediate request

**Andrea  Longo** · 2017-01-06 19:16 UTC

It's helpful to know more about the process, and what triggers an automated alert (beyond a mention) and what doesn't. I'm surprised there isn't more automation in the PR process.

**Andrea  Longo** · 2017-01-06 19:18 UTC

Certainly this isn't the same kind of environment that auto-nags when you haven't resolved an issue in the expected timeframe, but I figured some of that sort of tools might be available to manage incoming PRs. All I know about reviewing and merging PRs is the few I've done for GCI.

**Andrea  Longo** · 2017-01-06 19:19 UTC

I looked for something like this conversation in the docs, but only saw the PR section of the git guide.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-06 19:21 UTC

We should probably add a writeup of this stuff to do the docs. 

Basically GitHub sends a notification to people like me who "Watch" a repo whenever anyone posts a comment

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-06 19:21 UTC

(or opens/closes a PR or issue), which is how I stay on top of things

**Andrea  Longo** · 2017-01-06 19:30 UTC

Sounds like a repo watcher learns quickly to have good mail rules. I know I've got thousands of unread messages for the GCI repo, they got shoved in a folder as soon as I realized they consisted almost entirely of issue comments where I wasn't even an actual listed recipient of the message. (Unlike where I've subscribed.)

**Meet Mangukiya** · 2017-01-07 12:50 UTC

I have a suggestion, @Tim Abbott gitmate.io it can automate the labelling process

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-07 18:25 UTC

Yeah, we should check that out -- I think I actually heard about it from one of the authors at the GSoC summit and it sounded interesting

**Sumana Harihareswara** · 2017-01-11 17:08 UTC

## assignment policy?

*2017-01-07 to 2017-01-11 · 5 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/49-development-help/topic/assignment.20policy.3F/with/118818)*

**Meet Mangukiya** · 2017-01-07 12:36 UTC

How do we make sure that two person aren't working on same issue on zulip ?

**Adarsh S** · 2017-01-07 13:29 UTC

I don't think there's any dedicated tool to do that. People interested in solving an issue usually comments on that issue.

**Ayush Goyal** · 2017-01-07 13:40 UTC

Issues can be assigned to someone using GitHub

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-07 13:46 UTC

Right now our process for avoiding duplicate work on issues is kind of informal.  If you start to work on an issue, it's good to put a comment in the issue, and for small issues, there aren't likely to be collisions.  For any significant piece of work, it's good to come here (Zulip) and announce your intentions to work on some component.  This not only prevents duplicate work, but we can also steer you in the right direction of how to make the change, who to ask for advice, etc.

**Sumana Harihareswara** · 2017-01-11 17:25 UTC

@Meet Mangukiya does this answer your question?

@sinwar the `exclude` feature there only supports specific files; I think you want to add this to `help_markdown_rules`

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-09 15:19 UTC

Yep, @sinwar, rules that get added to `help_markdown_rules` only get applied to user help, which I believe is your intention here.  It works by virtue of this code:

~~~ py
456         for fn in by_lang['md']:
457             max_length = None
458             if fn not in markdown_docs_length_exclude:
459                 max_length = 120
460             rules = markdown_rules
461             if fn.startswith("templates/zerver/help"):
462                 rules = help_markdown_rules
463             if custom_check_file(fn, rules, max_length=max_length):
464                 failed = True

**Shayan Toqraee** · 2017-04-18 11:24 UTC

Hello.
I at last created the pull request.
Sorry for the long delay. I am very busy, and in between my work, I read a large portion of your docs, and also researched the topic (both took a lot of time).
I used the [UNICODE BIDIRECTIONAL ALGORITHM](http://www.unicode.org/reports/tr9/tr9-35.html) and the [UNICODE CHARACTER DATABASE](http://www.unicode.org/reports/tr44/tr44-18.html) to make sure the algorithm conforms to the standard.
For character ranges data, I at first wanted to use regex, but found out that `u` flag is added to the standard recently, and found no other way to write character literals which require more than 4 hexadecimal digits. So I used 92 characters to encode the character codes using simple base conversion (It can be converted to base-16 easily, but the size of the data would be about 1.7 times). Also, I am using binary search algorithm for finding out whether a character is in the ranges, which I think is more performant than using regex.
I wrote [this](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/b9/u6WhTV2l2PLCCZAU2zC5LA3e/UnicodeBiDiClassExtract.ps1) PowerShell script to extract the data. It can be run using newer versions of Windows PowerShell, or using PowerShellCore on many operating systems (see [this link](https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell/blob/master/docs/installation/linux.md) for installation instructions). It needs [UCD.zip](http://www.unicode.org/Public/9.0.0/ucd/UCD.zip) extracted next to it to work. And by the way, it is very slow, it takes some time for it to get done (for me, 1 minute to start writing output, and another 2 to finish it).
@Tim Abbott @Alicja Raszkowska @Sumana Harihareswara

I think a good next step might be to work on adding comments documenting what the various functions do as well as some unit tests in our node test suite (http://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/testing-with-node.html) for the functions you've added in #4535, and then we can merge those library functions as a useful prerequisite library.  

Next, there's probably 2 directions one could work on:
(1) Computing when to add the `dir` attributes on paragraphs, in the markdown processors.  One can do this in the Python process using a post-processing TreeProcessor to look at all the paragraph tags, call a function to determine the direction of the text in the paragraph.  One could probably start by doing the infrastructure work and having it just print the input and return False (would be mergable; True for testing) unconditionally just to make sure we have the right framework, and then work on making it correct.  https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/markdown.html is useful reading.  We care about the backend one more than the frontend to start, since it's authoritative.
(2) Hand-adding the `dir` attributes to (maybe even all?) paragraph tags, and get the CSS working happily to handle RTL messages.

I'm not sure which of those is the best next thing to do, but that should give you some ideas.

## mypy travis

*2017-01-14 to 2017-01-14 · 5 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/49-development-help/topic/mypy.20travis/with/127658)*

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-01-14 02:16 UTC

I have an error that was caught by mypy on travis but not mypy in vagrant .. is there something different between the two? The error was for something like 
```
def f(self, x=5):
    # type: (str, int) -> None
    pass
```

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-14 12:09 UTC

It may have been --py3?   You can run `./tools/run-mypy --py3` locally to catch errors that are version-dependent--often in these cases you should use Text instead of str.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-01-14 17:24 UTC

Thanks, error is in both py2 and py3. Also should have said explicitly, the error here is that self should not have a type, i.e. the correct thing is 
```
def f(self, x=5):
    # type: (int) -> None
    pass
```

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-14 18:00 UTC

Oh...yep...mypy basically ignores `self` in classes.  I'm not sure the exact reason, but basically `self` is sort of self-enforcing at runtime; you would have to bend over backward **not** to have `self` be the correct type, because Python's object syntax makes it happen naturally.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-14 18:58 UTC

@Rishi Gupta it could be that you haven't provisioned recently and Travis running with a slightly newer mypy (I upgraded it last week or so)

## JSON.stringify

*2017-01-18 to 2017-01-18 · 2 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/49-development-help/topic/JSON.2Estringify/with/131775)*

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-01-18 00:44 UTC

For hitting json endpoints from `admin.js` (e.g. via channel.post), it seems like we do a variety of things for `data`. Sometimes we do something like `data: { stream_name: stream_name}`, sometimes it's `data: { stream_name: JSON.stringify(stream_name)}`, and sometimes it looks more like `data: $(this).serialize()`. What's the difference/which is preferred? (Mostly asking the difference between the first two.)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-18 03:07 UTC

I think we mostly prefer  `JSON.stringify` on strings fields, whereas number are not stringified, and it's mostly due to the legacy of how our back end does validation/conversion of data.  In some parts of the code it may not be obvious that we're stringifying data, because it can happen in the callers and not right near the `channel.post` invocation.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-18 14:29 UTC

@Sumana Harihareswara It's pretty heavily built in to our system that you have one email per database installation.  Until we fix that, there are several workarounds, none of them ideal:
* Use a single realm with private streams.  (The drawback here is that all folks can still PM each other.)
* Have separate installations for each organization.
* Have users use emails like alice+1@example.com, alice+2@example.com
* Give users email accounts for each project.

It's interesting to hear this use case.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-18 19:31 UTC

Just hasn't been a use case that has been important to someone before now

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-18 19:31 UTC

We will probably add support for it in the next year regardless, but you could certainly accelerate that @Mike Daniel if it were important to you :)

## model.field names

*2017-01-21 to 2017-01-21 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/49-development-help/topic/model.2Efield.20names/with/134177)*

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-01-21 05:40 UTC

We seem to have a mix of tenses/moods in our field names. E.g. in Realm: 
* restricted_to_domain, invite_required, name_changes_disabled
* mandatory_topics
* show_digest_email, allow_message_editing

Any preferences for what we should use for new fields moving forward? (In particular, I'm debating between RealmAlias.allow_subdomains and RealmAlias.subdomains_allowed.)

**Sampriti Panda** · 2017-01-21 05:46 UTC

I think the second one reads better in code.

**Sampriti Panda** · 2017-01-21 05:46 UTC

e.g: `if realm.invite_required:`

**Sampriti Panda** · 2017-01-21 05:46 UTC

or `if realm_alias.subdomains_allowed():`

**Alex Dehnert** · 2017-01-21 06:42 UTC

Hm, I think I prefer allow_subdomains.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-21 13:57 UTC

If your field is a boolean, I prefer verb first.  `allow_subdomains` sounds more clearly like a boolean to me, whereas `subdomains_allowed` sounds possibly like a list of nouns.

**Alex Dehnert** · 2017-01-21 17:08 UTC

> allow_subdomains sounds more clearly like a boolean to me, whereas subdomains_allowed sounds possibly like a list of nouns.

==

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-21 17:17 UTC

It appears that all the examples from @Rishi Gupta are bools. Ideal names (for me) would be:
* restrict_emails
* require_invite
* allow_name_changes
* require_topics
* show_digest_email
* allow_message_editing

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-21 17:30 UTC

or maybe restricts_emails, requires_invite, allows_name_changes, requires_topics, etc.  (`if realm.restricts_emails:` reads kind of nicely)

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-01-21 19:43 UTC

Interesting, had not thought of the restricts_email possibility! I agree it reads nicely. 
My current thought is to use allow_subdomains, to keep the resemblance to some part of the codebase.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-21 19:47 UTC

Or `restrict_emails_to_domain` if we wanted it to be more explicit.

## postgres version

*2017-01-25 to 2017-01-25 · 14 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/49-development-help/topic/postgres.20version/with/136600)*

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-01-25 02:23 UTC

There is a Django 1.9 feature that relies on postgres version 9.4 or higher (jsonfield). It seems like we're currently on Postgres 9.3.14. Is an upgrade in the works?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-25 03:46 UTC

So here's the story: we use the default postgres on Trusty and Xenial.  So we use 9.5 on Xenial and 9.3 on Trusty.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-25 03:46 UTC

Nobody has worked on moving the Trusty systems to 9.5; the main annoying thing would be backporting the postgres packages

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-01-25 07:07 UTC

hm. I don't quite understand what's involved (e.g. random sites like https://www.tqhosting.com/kb/617/How-to-install-PostgreSQL-95-on-Ubuntu-1404-LTS-Trusty-Tahr.html suggest that it would "just work"), though it is not so important for the use being proposed.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-25 17:50 UTC

Looks like it involves adding the upstream Postgres apt repository

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-25 17:51 UTC

The main thing that we'd need to figure out how to do is migrate an existing Zulip server's database from using 9.3 to using 9.5

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-01-25 21:19 UTC

There does seem to be some indication that it is not hard if one doesn't mind (potentially hours of) downtime, e.g. [migrating 9.3 to 9.4](https://medium.com/@tk512/upgrading-postgresql-from-9-3-to-9-4-on-ubuntu-14-04-lts-2b4ddcd26535#.ixd85bz9j) and [9.4 to 9.5](https://blog.chaps.io/2016/02/08/upgrading-postgresql-from-9-4-to-9-5-on-ubuntu-15-10.html). Not sure if there are other pros to having everything on 9.5, e.g. for pgroonga or other things, or robustness issues in a simple upgrade script.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-25 22:55 UTC

There's also the valid approach of making new installs default to 9.5 (or even 9.6) but old ones stay on 9.3

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-01-25 23:01 UTC

That would still mean we couldn't use features in 9.5 though, right?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-25 23:13 UTC

correct. The reason to do that would be that it'd make our life easier when we do get to upgrading in 6 months (if that's what it is) for fewer folks to have to go through that process :)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-25 23:21 UTC

That seems like a good idea.  @Rishi Gupta When you say the upgrade would take potentially hours of downtime, is that speculation on your part?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-25 23:23 UTC

I presume it depends on the size of the database, and is a data point from postgres docs?

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-01-25 23:26 UTC

yeah, mainly a line from the link above:
9.3->9.4: "On a 17GB cluster it took an hour so be aware of this."

From a style perspective, we probably want to restructure emoji.js to not access other modules until `emoji.initialize()`

OK we just deployed a further revision to the emoji support which removes basically all the duplicate emoji (yay!).  Testing appreciated (one thing to look at is old messages).  Problems that are known are:
* If you send a message containing emoji using one of the removed aliases (e.g. `:angry_face:`, it'll still render that emoji, but local echo will not render properly so there will be a slight flicker before the final correct render.).  Basically the JS and backend implementations disagree about which emoji codes exist; backend is more liberal.

does it ever make sense to change jquery selectors (e.g. $('#moo')) to document.getElementbyId('#moo')? I know the latter is supposed to be 10s of times faster, but I don't know if it's in the microsecond range or the millisecond range. The situation is I have a bar graph (/stats page) with a hover event on each bar, and each hover is currently calling ~5 jquery selectors. I'm trying to figure out why it feels a bit laggy when you run your mouse over the graph.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-07 05:12 UTC

For analytics stuff I'd be a little more aggressive about avoiding jQuery overhead, even to just get the simple speedup of not going through jQuery.  But often the slowdown can be due to an overly complex selector and not mere jQuery encapsulation overhead.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-07 05:13 UTC

Usually it doesn't matter what you do with selectors as long as you're not doing it in a loop, but a hover sorta can become a loop if you're moving quickly; I'd recommend profiling.  Debouncing might also be what you need here...

beb3782e6c64366af0a27195e483dfab5223da0c is a recent fix that I made that hugely sped up things; it may be instructive for the analytics stuff

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-09 21:29 UTC

And then I usually start with `git rebase -i master`.  If you simply have a bunch of extraneous commits, you can usually safely delete them in the interactive rebase.

**Andrea  Longo** · 2017-02-09 21:29 UTC

I have several commits already that I'd rather not throw away, is there a way to move just those to a new branch?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-09 21:31 UTC

Generally git is additive--every time you do something in git, you're just creating new commit histories.  The only danger of rebasing is that your old commit can get "lost" in terms of not having a branch attacthed to it.  But it's still there in `git reflog`.   And you can "back up" in git by attaching a branch name to your current commit.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-09 21:32 UTC

Have you read the "Back to the Future" git metaphor?

**Andrea  Longo** · 2017-02-09 21:33 UTC

Yeah, time travel is messy.

**Andrea  Longo** · 2017-02-09 21:34 UTC

I found a few things about making a new branch and then removing some latest offending commits from the original. But then the new branch is still the same.

**Andrea  Longo** · 2017-02-09 21:35 UTC

This is sounding like it's easier to re-do my changes. It's not much, but I was trying to do a bunch of individual changes to the same doc as separate commits so I could keep track of what areas of the doc I had updated already.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-09 21:42 UTC

Yeah, sometimes it's easier to re-do.  But you definitely want to get comfortable with rebasing.  When you create a branch with `git branch foo`, it labels your current head commit, but it doesn't make `foo` the tracking branch, so when you rebase, you'll still be affecting the `bar` branch.  But `git branch` is useful to create a backup label of your commit.  Branches are essentially just "names" for commits, with the main nuance being that your "current" branch will keep tracking to new commits you make, or rebases that you execute.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-09 21:45 UTC

The BTTF example:

~~~
git branch known-dystopia-where-biff-is-millionaire
git rebase -i marty-arrives-in-future
# delete the buy-almanac commit
~~~

Presumably at the end of this things are good, but if something manages to get even worse, you can go back to the original branch.  (Yes, it's a very strained metaphor.)

**Raghav Jajodia** · 2017-02-24 02:28 UTC

I have encountered this "error: Unsupported target for indexed assignment" at https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/3424/files#diff-96ea148dcd22c60ffdb097f113d5e4aaR389 and i am not sure how to fix this.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-24 02:42 UTC

This seems to me to be a bug with mypy, but you can work around it by rewriting the section as follows, which I think is cleaner anyway:

~~~ py
 375     bot = dict(email=user_profile.email,
 376                user_id=user_profile.id,
 377                full_name=user_profile.full_name,
 378                api_key=user_profile.api_key,
 379                default_sending_stream=default_sending_stream_name,
 380                default_events_register_stream=default_events_register_stream_name,
 381                default_all_public_streams=user_profile.default_all_public_streams,
 382                avatar_url=avatar_url(user_profile),
 383                )
 384     # Set the owner key only when the bot has an owner.
 385     # The default bots don't have an owner. So don't
 386     # set the owner key while reactivating them.
 387     if user_profile.bot_owner is not None:
 388         bot['owner'] = user_profile.bot_owner.email
 389 
 390     event = dict(type="realm_bot", op="add", bot=bot)

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-24 02:47 UTC

Hmm.  Usually mypy errors of that form result from reusing a variable with different types in a given function

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-24 02:47 UTC

But I don't see that here

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-24 02:47 UTC

Steve's suggestion makes sense to me

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-24 02:49 UTC

Yeah, I feel like we have similar code in other places, and I don't see why mypy can't make what seems like an obvious type inference here.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-24 02:54 UTC

yeah, agreed.  I would actually report a mypy bug for that if we can make a clean reproducer

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-24 03:05 UTC

This is the simplified case:

~~~ py
 390     foo = dict(junk=1, bar=dict(yo=3))
 391     foo['bar']['yo'] = 5

```
(?!^|\s)(\$\$[^_$][^$]*\$\$)(?=$|\s)

Which, in human-understandable language means: "find anything surrounded by double dollar signs, that doesn't start with an underscore. It sould be a single word, too (e.g. surrounded by spaces or start/end of the string)"

These are example matches:

```
this is $$a match$$
$$match$$
matching $$is$$ good
```

```
got $$ in my pocket
foo$$bar$$foo
foo $$_$$ bar
```

## emoji: Replace compose emoji picker

*2017-03-21 to 2017-03-21 · 15 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/49-development-help/topic/emoji.3A.20Replace.20compose.20emoji.20picker/with/175634)*

**Tejas Kasetty** · 2017-03-21 11:33 UTC

@Rishi Gupta 
      Can you give me more insight about the issue [#4122](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/4122)? 
       What is the expected and the purpose.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-21 11:35 UTC

I think the main goal at first is to consolidate the two UIs, so that we don't have two separate UIs for essentially the same thing, which is picking an emoji.  Once we have one emoji-picker widget, we can start building more advanced features on top of it, and it will improve both the compose experience and the reaction experience.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-21 11:40 UTC

One of the challenges is that you're gonna want the same basic widget for both use cases, but clicking on the emojis will result in different actions.  You'll probably want to split out a module that basically draws the widget, and then have some mechanism to set up callbacks according to the context.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-21 11:42 UTC

A good way to get started is to read the code and see if there are some basic cleanups you can do on the reactions code in popovers.js.

**Tejas Kasetty** · 2017-03-21 11:46 UTC

Awesome , the idea is interesting and exciting.  So, basically the emoji we use in the compose box is  the compose emoji  picker and the one we use as a drop down present for each persons message is the emoji reactions picker. And two different UIs are being used with two implementations so, and if there is a modification in one then we have to separately modify the other one as well. so, the fix is unifying them to a single UI. Am i getting it right?

**Tejas Kasetty** · 2017-03-21 11:49 UTC

I will have to start of  with code. Check for places with CEP (compose emoji picker ) and ERP (reactions picker) and try to create a single implementation  for both but differences in action based on context whether its being used in message composition or as reaction

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-21 11:50 UTC

yep!

## mocking queue_json_publish

*2017-03-24 to 2017-03-24 · 12 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/49-development-help/topic/mocking.20queue_json_publish/with/178484)*

**Vaibhav Singhal** · 2017-03-24 17:51 UTC

I was writing tests and in that I was trying to mock queue_json_publish. So I gave it's address (zerver.lib.queue.queue_json_publish) to mock.patch but it wasn't getting mocked. Then I saw another test, of email mirror, there the address given was where it was called in source code. So I tried to repeat this and then I was successful. What is the reason behind this?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-24 17:56 UTC

This is due to how Python works.  Even though there may only be one implementation of some function, it can be bound to different names in different namespaces, where the namespaces are generally modules.

When you use mock libraries, they only re-bind one of the names, so it requires some subtle understanding of how Python works to re-bind the correct name and stub out the real implementation.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-24 17:57 UTC

And your hunch that "the address where it was called in source code" is what matters is basically the answer.  You want to make sure that you re-bind the name that would come up during the codepath your test exercises.

**Vaibhav Singhal** · 2017-03-24 18:00 UTC

for future, If suppose a function makes use of 2 modules, each of which uses this function, so to mock queue_json_publish, will I have to mock it twice? for each module?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-24 18:02 UTC

Yeah, you'd have to mock it twice

**Vaibhav Singhal** · 2017-03-24 18:02 UTC

okay, understood

**Vaibhav Singhal** · 2017-03-24 18:05 UTC

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_AEJHKGk9ns&t=1359s

**Vaibhav Singhal** · 2017-03-24 18:13 UTC

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-03-25 19:31 UTC

How much space (over the network) would sending an array of 10000 zeros (in response to an ajax request) take? Should I think of it as 4 bytes per number = 40kb? Or would it somehow be compressed?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-25 19:54 UTC

Most compression algorithms will deal with this well:

~~~
>>> gzip.open('/tmp/test.txt', 'w').write('0' * 10000)
10000
>>> open('/tmp/test.txt').read()
"\x1f\x8b\x08\x08\xa1\xca\xd6X\x02\xfftest.txt\x00\xed\xc1\x01\r\x00\x00\x00\xc2\xa0J\xef\x9f\xce\x1cn@\x01\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\xc0\xbf\x01iX\x18\n\x10'\x00\x00"

**Aditya Bansal** · 2017-03-25 19:58 UTC

Is such a thing (gzip) implemented by default while making requests over network?

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-03-25 19:59 UTC

It's going to be just over 20000 bytes:

If sent type "application/json", then it'll be expressed roughly as `"{'key':[0,0,0,0,0,...]}"`, which will roughly be 10000 bytes of `0`, 9999 bytes of `,`, two bytes for `[]` and the key.

However, if this is gzipped by the server, in particular this example is like ~60 bytes because gzip heavily optimizes the repetition of the zeros. It won't work nearly as well with any other combo of number of course however since the entropy will be higher.

[The gzipped version from node is 61 bytes it seems.](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/56/8oUD2putYGAefqSDvoYijq_f/Screen-Shot-2017-03-25-at-12.58.01-PM.png)

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-03-25 20:00 UTC

What would 10000 zeros be sent for?

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-03-25 20:10 UTC

[You can see in the response headers from our server that content is sent gzipped.](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/89/ckdgdUEFYBcQl2y9YMuCQUL8/Screen-Shot-2017-03-25-at-1.09.24-PM.png) It's not something done by default but most servers are configured to do it, as is ours.

**Aditya Bansal** · 2017-03-25 20:16 UTC

yeah some kind of compression must be good.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-03-25 20:17 UTC

cool, thanks!
A lot of our analytics endpoints return large blocks of 0s, and in particular I'm considering adding one that will always return [0]*(number of hours the realm has been around) to simplify some code.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-03-25 20:19 UTC

also, nice estimate on the 20000 bytes; I tested it on the dev environment and it indeed is 19.6kb and 196kb for 100000 zeros.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-03-25 20:19 UTC

Though I'm still a bit puzzled why the 0s aren't four bytes each

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-03-25 20:33 UTC

Because everything is cast to a JSON string it'll be the literal length of number in bytes, so even though 1000000 could be expressed as Int32, it'll take up 56 bytes.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-03-25 20:34 UTC

ahh, got it

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-25 21:21 UTC

Despite the effectiveness of compression algorithms, it's probably still a good idea to consider some sort of sparse representation of the data.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-26 23:27 UTC

Your first step to debug this should be to run `./tools/test-js-with-node` locally, to see if you get the same failure.  Then run the same thing on HEAD^, to see if the problem preceded your change.

It's possible that you rebased off a temporarily broken master, in which case you'll want to re-fetch code and rebase off a newer copy of master.

**Jonathan Pan** · 2017-03-27 00:25 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-27 00:29 UTC

One thing I noticed is that you don't use return true/false in all places.  The way our hotkey system works is that the big function should return true/false immediately if it has figured out how to handle a code, and we only do  `preventDefault()`in the click handlers.

Before spending too much time debugging this, I would consider extracting a lot of your logic out to a separate function, which is probably a good idea regardless of the node tests.

We eventually want most of your changes to be in `drafts.js`, actually, and `hotkeys.js` should only be a dumb dispatcher.

**Jonathan Pan** · 2017-03-27 00:33 UTC

Okay, will try that. I'm using `preventDefault()` to stop automatic scrolling when the user presses the arrow keys.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-27 00:33 UTC

It's also generally good practice to check for the hotkey in the outer conditional and check for UI stuff in the inner conditionals.  If drafts only need to handle a few hotkeys--up, down, and maybe backspace--we don't want to deal with all the complexities of the draft UI for other keys that are pressed.  This is partly driven by performance--the hotkey handler runs for almost every keystroke in the app, so we need to be thoughtful there--but it is even more driven by reliability (let's not break any other keys than we have to if we introduce a bug accidentally).

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-27 00:33 UTC

The caller should call `preventDefault` if you simply return true.

**Jonathan Pan** · 2017-03-27 01:14 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-27 01:15 UTC

ok, keep debugging :smile:

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-27 01:31 UTC

Let us know if you're truly stumped, but you can probably keep debugging this by gradually undoing your changes.  You can use `git commit -am 'wip'` to create checkpoints.  You can use `git checkout .` to roll back.

**Jonathan Pan** · 2017-03-27 02:20 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-27 02:22 UTC

Yeah, that was probably the right way to fix it.  It was sort of a strange symptom, but it may have been an artifact of not checking the key in the outer conditional combined with our exception handling in the tests not specifically catching assert errors.  We should tighten up the latter problem.
