## strip multiple chars together

*2017-04-04 to 2017-04-06 · 8 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/49-development-help/topic/strip.20multiple.20chars.20together/with/184865)*

**Yago González** · 2017-04-04 21:02 UTC

So the `strip()` Python function allows you to remove characters at the ends of strings. You can put a string as an argument, whose characters will be the ones to remove (no matter the order).

What are your suggestions for doing this with a group of characters in a specific order? For example:

~~~py
>>> 'ABfooBA'.strip('AB')
'foo'
~~~

What if I wanted that to return `fooBA`?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-04 21:18 UTC

Use startswith or endswith, and then slice it.  I am not aware of a shorter way, but I think the two line or four line idioms are commonly used here.

**Yago González** · 2017-04-04 21:29 UTC

And if multiple matches are possible, something like `while text.startswith(...)`, right?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-04 21:31 UTC

Yep, although I am curious what the context is here.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-04-04 22:10 UTC

I tihnk there's an `lstrip` and `rstrip`?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-04-04 22:13 UTC

Those still are by-character, not by-substring

**Yago González** · 2017-04-06 17:19 UTC

Steve, about the context you mentioned:

Sometimes we've got newlines at the ends of our i18n strings, which is a bit messy when working in Transifex.

A simple `strip()` should work here, but it turns out that the newlines are escaped (i.e. `\\n`) and as far as I've seen it's more difficult to do the stripping before escaping those.

**Yago González** · 2017-04-06 17:19 UTC

Hence, I need to remove the whole `\\n` substring at both ends.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-04-20 04:58 UTC

`group-pm-with` isn't finished or documented yet, but the intent it for it to be "a group PM conversation containing both you and the other person".  Whereas `pm-with` accepts a list of users, and is the specific 1:1 or group PM conversation including that person.

**Shayan Toqraee** · 2017-04-20 11:50 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-04-20 17:23 UTC

Yeah, I'm not sure this is your fault that this is confusing.  The plan is that `pm-with` is exact, `group-pm-with` is for when you want to look at all group PM threads that _include_ a person (or persons), whereas `pm-with` is intended for when you want a specific thread.

I think that this experience is a good argument for changing the `group-pm-with` name, since this is kinda confusing to explain :)

Maybe we should just do something like `pm:` and `pm-including:` for these 2 concepts?

## suggestions for field name

*2017-04-19 to 2017-06-13 · 85 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/49-development-help/topic/suggestions.20for.20field.20name/with/189874)*

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-04-19 19:23 UTC

Would `emoji_codepoint` be a good name for a field in Reaction model? This field is to be used to store the unicode codepoint of emoji used in reaction.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-04-19 19:28 UTC

Will the field also be used for the name of a realm emoji?  Or how are we handling that?

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-04-19 19:30 UTC

The realm emoji thing had slipped from my mind.

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-04-19 19:31 UTC

Need to think more about it then.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-04-19 19:32 UTC

I guess one question is whether we want to use the same field name for realm emoji as normal emoji codepoints

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-04-19 19:33 UTC

I could imagine namespacing things where realm emoji start with some special character sequence in this representation so that there are no name conflicts

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-04-19 19:37 UTC

We can use a flag to indicate whether the emoji is realm emoji or not(`is_realm_emoji` for example) and add an `emoji` field that will hold the emoji codepoint in case of normal emojis and emoji name in case of realm emojis. Does that make sense?

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-04-19 21:47 UTC

>I guess one question is whether we want to use the same field name for realm emoji as normal emoji codepoints

I am thinking of using the same field for storing the codepoint as well as realm emoji name.

>I could imagine namespacing things where realm emoji start with some special character sequence in this representation so that there are no name conflicts

Are you talking about conflicts between unicode codepoint of normal emojis and realm emoji name?
@Tim Abbott

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-04-19 22:25 UTC

yep, that's the potential conflict!

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-04-19 22:41 UTC

What could be a good name for the field? For prefix, I am able to think of `REP_` (Realm Emoji Prefix).

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-04-19 22:42 UTC

We generally prefer spelled-out names over acronyms, since acronyms can make the codebase unapproachable

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-04-19 22:43 UTC

@Rishi Gupta do you have ideas for what we should call this?

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-04-19 22:43 UTC

> We generally prefer spelled-out names over acronyms, since acronyms can make the codebase unapproachable
okay

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-04-20 00:12 UTC

Possibly the overlap is a feature, not a bug? I guess a few questions:
* Say a realm uploads an emoji called "airplane". Should that replace :airplane: for everyone (regardless of which emoji set they are using)? I feel like the answer is yes.
* Say a realm uploads an emoji called "u2708". Should that replace :airplane: (and all other alternate shortcodes) for everyone? I feel like the answer is yes here as well.

Do we know what slack does?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-04-20 04:56 UTC

yeah, I think I agree that the overlap is probably a feature; so maybe we don't need a special encoding, and we should just call it something like "codepoint" or "value" or something.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-04-20 07:13 UTC

Mild preference for codepoint, despite the confusion between unicode and realm codepoints. 
Also Reaction.value could plausibly mean the number of people that clicked that Reaction (if you saw it out of context).

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-04-20 17:21 UTC

OK let's just go with codepoint.  We can always change it later :)

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-06-12 17:56 UTC

@Tim Abbott pointed out in comment(https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/5141#pullrequestreview-42706840) that codepoint doesn't seem to be a correct name for this field as it is actually a string of series of codepoints. A few other suggestion for the field name are 'codepoint_string', 'emoji_code' etc. What do folks here think would be good one?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-12 17:56 UTC

@Greg Price may have thoughts on this one :)

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-12 17:56 UTC

I think we should try to make a decision on this today

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-12 17:57 UTC

(I have to go AFK for a bit though)

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-06-12 17:58 UTC

cc: @Rishi Gupta ^^

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-06-12 18:00 UTC

what do these codepoint/codepoint_strings look like?

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-06-12 18:01 UTC

These are actually string of hexadecimal numbers separated by hyphens

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-06-12 18:02 UTC

Like 1f1ec-1f1e7

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-06-12 18:03 UTC

I think I'm fine with calling that a codepoint, but maybe am not understanding the details of the issue yet :).

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-06-12 18:12 UTC

I think the main concern here is that in unicode terminology a codepoint is a single numerical value assigned to a particular character but here our field is not a numerical value rather a string representation of series of codepoints.

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-06-12 18:50 UTC

@Tim Abbott you had also mentioned in the comment that you are not sure whether we should drop the emoji_name field or not. I don't see a use case for keeping the emoji_name in the model as we will now be displaying reactions using canonical names and not using what user chose.

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-12 21:44 UTC

Yeah, it shouldn't be "codepoint" because it's a list of codepoints -- just like a field that's a string shouldn't have the name "char"

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-12 21:46 UTC

It's often just one, and in earlier eras of how emoji worked on the Internet I think one emoji was just one codepoint, but now there are lots of emoji that are represented as several codepoints

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-06-12 21:47 UTC

yeah and situation becomes even worse with zwj sequences :)

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-12 21:48 UTC

Huh, what are those?

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-12 21:49 UTC

Looking at this field and thinking about what to call it -- it's a field on a `Reaction` object, which is an emoji reaction, and specifically it seems like it's the field that identifies what emoji the reaction is with, at least when `is_realm_emoji` is false

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-06-12 21:49 UTC

https://emojipedia.org/emoji-zwj-sequences/

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-12 21:50 UTC

I don't really understand what happens or what this field means when `is_realm_emoji` is true -- @Harshit Bansal , what goes in this field in that case? (Or is there something I should read about that?)

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-12 21:50 UTC

Ah yes -- yeah, that's a common pattern that composes one emoji out of a sequence of several codepoints

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-06-12 21:51 UTC

If `is_realm_emoji` is true this field currently stores the name of the realm emoji used in the reaction

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-06-12 21:51 UTC

Though we will shortly switch it to use realm_emoji's id

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-12 21:52 UTC

That is, this field will contain an ID into the realm emoji table?

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-12 21:53 UTC

So really the specifics of how this field is interpreted are quite different in two different cases

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-06-12 21:53 UTC

Yep but it is not decided yet, for now we are going to use to store realm emoji name

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-06-12 21:53 UTC

> So really the specifics of how this field is interpreted are quite different in two different cases
Yeah

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-12 21:53 UTC

It seems like what's in common between both these cases is that it's an identifier for the emoji

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-12 21:54 UTC

Which in the Unicode case (the non-realm-emoji case) is a particular string representation of the sequence of codepoints involved

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-06-12 21:54 UTC

yeah

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-12 21:54 UTC

A representation that we made up ourselves, is it? Does this hyphen-separated-hex format have a name or do people use it elsewhere?

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-06-12 21:56 UTC

No we haven't made it ourselves, it is used in iamcal's dataset which we use as a data source for our emojis.

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-12 21:56 UTC

Ah cool, good to know

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-12 21:56 UTC

I think I'd call this field something like `emoji_id`, or `emoji_code`

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-06-12 21:57 UTC

I too like `emoji_code` :)

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-12 21:57 UTC

I'd also put it after `is_realm_emoji`, not before it -- because its meaning is totally dependent on the value of that field, like it's in a different namespace depending on that field

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-12 21:58 UTC

There should also be a comment in the model -- maybe better yet, a discussion in the developer docs somewhere and just a one-line comment there pointing to the docs -- about what that field means

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-12 21:59 UTC

That in the Unicode / non-realm case, it's the codepoints in iamcal's format, with a link if possible to that dataset's description of the format

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-06-12 22:00 UTC

Currently we don't have no description in docs regarding this, for now I think I will put a comment describing the field and later when we update our documentation regarding emoji we can add a link to it

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-12 22:00 UTC

Seems reasonable

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-12 22:01 UTC

Hmm, one question zooming out a bit: will we definitely only ever have these two kinds of emoji? Or could there be a third in the future?

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-12 22:01 UTC

I wonder if `is_realm_emoji` should be an enum instead

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-12 22:01 UTC

Like `emoji_type`, with values `UNICODE` or `REALM`

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-12 22:02 UTC

It might be good to go to an enum for purely stylistic reasons now, but I don't think we need to future-proof anything, since we're not dealing with a ton of data.

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-06-12 22:03 UTC

I don't think that there can be a third type of emojis.

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-06-12 22:03 UTC

I mean I wonder what it would represent

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-12 22:04 UTC

Yeah, I agree with Steve -- I think the enum may be clearer even though it will probably only ever be two values

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-12 22:05 UTC

Or even if it's only ever two values, rather

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-12 22:06 UTC

I do think it's reasonably likely that in 5 years there'll be some other whole family of emoji that isn't made up separately by people in each realm, so it doesn't fit as realm emoji, but also for whatever reason isn't described by sequences of Unicode codepoints

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-12 22:07 UTC

That'd be a little sad because it's the Unicode dream that all text should be representable in one interoperable, reasonably uniform system, but could happen

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-12 22:07 UTC

But as Steve says, it's not a ton of data so we can always do a migration later, and so that part isn't an important reason for things now

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-06-12 22:09 UTC

We do have a this kind of emoji, our `:zulip:` emoji :zulip:, which is not made up separately by people in each realm but it is realm emoji.

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-06-12 22:10 UTC

We don't store it in the RealmEmoji table but rather fake it to be a realm emoji.

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-06-12 22:11 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-12 22:12 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2017-06-12 22:13 UTC

But you could imagine out in the world of emoji someone having a bright idea that results in thousands of new emoji in some new system -- and then we'd probably want to handle it in a different more systematic way

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-06-12 22:13 UTC

yeah anything is possible

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-06-13 00:25 UTC

Adding a +1 to `emoji_code`

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-13 03:44 UTC

`emoji_code` wfm as well

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-13 05:51 UTC

@Harshit Bansal as a quick comment on `emoji_name`, there's an argument that if an emoji gets renamed in some future update of our emoji data, we want to store what the name the user clicked on was, not the name that icon eventually changes to have.  Which is why we might want to keep the `emoji_name` field, but only use it for the title attribute.

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-06-13 06:20 UTC

from io import StringIO
from typing import Any, TypeAlias, TypedDict

from django.apps import apps
from django.core.management import call_command
from django.db import DEFAULT_DB_ALIAS

    ("zerver", "0012_remove_appledevicetoken"),
    ("zerver", "0013_realmemoji"),
    ("zerver", "0014_realm_emoji_url_length"),
    ("zerver", "0015_attachment"),
    ("zerver", "0016_realm_create_stream_by_admins_only"),
    ("zerver", "0017_userprofile_bot_type"),
    ("zerver", "0018_realm_emoji_message"),
    ("zerver", "0019_preregistrationuser_realm_creation"),
    ("zerver", "0020_add_tracking_attachment"),
    ("zerver", "0021_migrate_attachment_data"),
    ("zerver", "0022_subscription_pin_to_top"),
    ("zerver", "0023_userprofile_default_language"),
    ("zerver", "0024_realm_allow_message_editing"),
    ("zerver", "0025_realm_message_content_edit_limit"),
    ("zerver", "0026_delete_mituser"),
    ("zerver", "0027_realm_default_language"),
    ("zerver", "0028_userprofile_tos_version"),
    # This migration was in python-social-auth, and was mistakenly removed
    # from its `replaces` in
    # https://github.com/python-social-auth/social-app-django/pull/25
    ("default", "0005_auto_20160727_2333"),
    # This was a typo (twofactor for two_factor) corrected in
    # https://github.com/jazzband/django-two-factor-auth/pull/642
    ("twofactor", "0001_squashed_0008_delete_phonedevice"),
]


def get_migration_status(**options: Any) -> str:
    verbosity = options.get("verbosity", 1)

    for app_config in apps.get_app_configs():
        if module_has_submodule(app_config.module, "management"):
            import_module(".management", app_config.name)

    app_label = options["app_label"] if options.get("app_label") else None
    db = options.get("database", DEFAULT_DB_ALIAS)
    out = StringIO()
    command_args = ["--list"]
    if app_label:
        command_args.append(app_label)

    call_command(
        "showmigrations",
        *command_args,
        database=db,
        no_color=options.get("no_color", False),
        settings=options.get("settings", os.environ["DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE"]),
        stdout=out,
        skip_checks=options.get("skip_checks", True),
        traceback=options.get("traceback", True),
        verbosity=verbosity,
    )
    out.seek(0)
    output = out.read()
    return re.sub(r"\x1b\[[0-9;]*m", "", output)


def clean_parsed_migration_status(
    migrations_dict: AppMigrations, stale_migrations: list[tuple[str, str]] = STALE_MIGRATIONS
) -> AppMigrations:
    for app, stale_migration in stale_migrations:
        installed_app = migrations_dict.get(app)
        if installed_app:
            updated_app_migrations = [
                mig for mig in installed_app if not mig.endswith(stale_migration)
            ]
            if len(updated_app_migrations) > 0:
                migrations_dict[app] = updated_app_migrations
            else:
                migrations_dict.pop(app)
    return migrations_dict


def parse_migration_status(migration_status_print: str) -> AppMigrations:
    lines = migration_status_print.strip().split("\n")
    migrations_dict: AppMigrations = {}
    current_app = None
    migration_line_prefix = ("[X]", "[ ]", "[-]", "(no migrations)")
    for line in lines:
        line = line.strip()
        if not line.startswith(migration_line_prefix) and line:
            current_app = line
            migrations_dict[current_app] = []
        elif line.startswith(migration_line_prefix):
            assert current_app is not None
            migrations_dict[current_app].append(line)

    return clean_parsed_migration_status(migrations_dict)
```

+def get_migration_status(**options: Any) -> str:
+    verbosity = options.get("verbosity", 1)
+
+    for app_config in apps.get_app_configs():
+        if module_has_submodule(app_config.module, "management"):
+            import_module(".management", app_config.name)
+
+    app_label = options["app_label"] if options.get("app_label") else None
+    db = options.get("database", DEFAULT_DB_ALIAS)
+    out = StringIO()
+    command_args = ["--list"]
+    if app_label:
+        command_args.append(app_label)
+
+    call_command(
+        "showmigrations",
+        *command_args,
+        database=db,
+        no_color=options.get("no_color", False),
+        settings=options.get("settings", os.environ["DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE"]),
+        stdout=out,
+        skip_checks=options.get("skip_checks", True),
+        traceback=options.get("traceback", True),
+        verbosity=verbosity,
+    )
+    out.seek(0)
+    output = out.read()
+    return re.sub(r"\x1b\[[0-9;]*m", "", output)

+def clean_parsed_migration_status(
+    migrations_dict: AppMigrations, stale_migrations: list[tuple[str, str]] = STALE_MIGRATIONS
+) -> AppMigrations:
+    for app, stale_migration in stale_migrations:
+        installed_app = migrations_dict.get(app)
+        if installed_app:
+            updated_app_migrations = [
+                mig for mig in installed_app if not mig.endswith(stale_migration)
+            ]
+            if len(updated_app_migrations) > 0:
+                migrations_dict[app] = updated_app_migrations
+            else:
+                migrations_dict.pop(app)
+    return migrations_dict
+
+
+def parse_migration_status(migration_status_print: str) -> AppMigrations:
+    lines = migration_status_print.strip().split("\n")
+    migrations_dict: AppMigrations = {}
+    current_app = None
+    migration_line_prefix = ("[X]", "[ ]", "[-]", "(no migrations)")
+    for line in lines:
+        line = line.strip()
+        if not line.startswith(migration_line_prefix) and line:
+            current_app = line
+            migrations_dict[current_app] = []
+        elif line.startswith(migration_line_prefix):
+            assert current_app is not None
+            migrations_dict[current_app].append(line)
+
+    return clean_parsed_migration_status(migrations_dict)

**Steve Howell** · 2025-01-17 12:59 UTC

Interesting stuff.  The one bug that I have seen with Python coverage tools is that `continue` statements often cause false alarms.  I don't think that's immediately relevant to what @Pieter K is reporting, but it's hopefully kind of on topic.

The Python coverage tools are generally quite predictable and deterministic, but there are certain situations where the Python interpreter kind of "outsmarts" the coverage tools, for lack of a better word.  If you have a continue statement in Python, then Python is sometimes smart enough to kind of optimize it away, which is good for the running code, but bad for coverage reports.  In that case the normal workaround is to just extract a function and change `continue` to `return`, and that change often improves the code anyway.

I suspect the stopgap solution here is probably at least not detrimental to the code, and it may even be an improvement.  Nice job tracking this down!

**Steve Howell** · 2025-01-17 13:10 UTC

I suspect  #33063  is actually an upstream problem of Zulip, and it has something to do with the interaction between the Python interpreter and the coverage tools. I believe that Zulip still uses the coverage tools originally written by Ned Batchelder. https://nedbatchelder.com/blog/202411/coveragepy_originally.html is a good reference.  @Pieter K if you really want to do a deep dive on this, you can contribute to the overall Python community by extracting some kind of small test case for this that transcends Zulip.  But I also think it's just fine to move on with the stopgap, and it's just one of those things programmers have to deal with.

**Matthias** · 2017-05-04 13:45 UTC

Hi Jim, that question belongs into a different topic but I believe it's neither. I'm not the expert but I think it uses its own.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-04 13:45 UTC

@Jim Zulip has its own messaging protocol.  You basically make an HTTP connection to the server and call the `/json/events` endpoint, and then you receive payloads that correspond to Zulip events, such as messages being delivered to you, notifications that users are now "present," updates on newly created streams, etc.

**Jim** · 2017-05-04 13:46 UTC

thank you for your reply

**Jim** · 2017-05-04 13:46 UTC

but is it based on any known protocols?

**Jim** · 2017-05-04 13:47 UTC

or was it developed from scratch ?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-04 13:47 UTC

Also, messages are obviously "distributed" in some sense, but we also have a central database (Postgres) that stores all the messages.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-04 13:48 UTC

The stream/topic model is very roughly based on Zephyr, but the implementation was essentially from scratch.  @Tim Abbott can give more details on this in the next couple hours.  Basically, Zulip was not based on prior protocols, because prior protocols didn't really accomodate the "topic" concept very well.

```
setTimeout(function () {
                 $('.emoji-popover-filter').focus();
                 $('.emoji-popover-filter').caret(Infinity);
             }, 0);
```
The issue is to bring the cursor to the end of the entered search string when navigated using hotkeys in emoji reactions picker.
The problem is focus. On focusing the, cursor would move to the starting position so have set the cursor to end.

But if this is not put in setTimeout as callback. The time when the focus is executed is usually after the cursor position is set. This is because of how the web APIs are handled. The order of evaluation should made in such a way that the cursor position is set and soon after focus . This is important because if the execution is interleaved, we can see the cursor flicker. To prevent this, I used setTimeout. Does anybody have any idea how to do it without setTimeout.

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-05-08 17:26 UTC

Am looking at this now.

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-05-08 17:58 UTC

The `setTimeout` seems to not be necessary.

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-05-08 17:58 UTC

Firstly, change the two lines to:

```js
$('.emoji-popover-filter').focus().caret(Infinity);
```

You're re-querying a selector for nothing.

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-05-08 18:05 UTC

Then, just return `true` after this, since you've successfully performed the action. Then it won't call focus below which is what is preventing your code from running.

It should just look like this:

```js
if (selected_emoji && selected_index < 6) { // move up into reaction filter
    $('.emoji-popover-filter').focus().caret(Infinity);
    return true;
}
```

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-05-08 18:18 UTC

Btw, you're somewhat correct @Tejas Kasetty that normal events are not guaranteed to fall in the order you expect, but events generated **in browser** I believe ARE guaranteed. You can safely assume on the next line of code that the event has happened.

Here's a fiddle to show it:

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-05-08 18:18 UTC

https://jsfiddle.net/x6x1bx20/

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-05-08 18:18 UTC

You can see that when you trigger a click, the onclick events run immediately so that on the fifth line where we log the counter, it is already 4.

**Tejas Kasetty** · 2017-05-09 01:33 UTC

        'realm': {
            'uri': 'https://chat.zulip.org',
            'name': 'Zulip Community',
        },
        'device_info': {
            'login_time': "12/12/12, 12:12:12",
            'device_browser': "Firefox",
            'device_os': "ZulipOS",
            'device_ip': '127.0.0.1',
        },
        'referrer': {
            'full_name': 'Zooly Zulipson',
            'email': 'zooly@zulip.org',
        },
        'user': {
            'full_name': 'Zooly Zulipson',
            'email': 'zooly@zulip.org',
        },
        'referrer_name': 'Zooly Zulipson',
        'referrer_email': 'Zooly Zulipson',
        'realm_uri': 'https://chat.zulip.org',
        'server_uri': 'https://chat.zulip.org',
        'old_email': 'oldmail@zulip.org',
        'new_email': 'newmail@zulip.org',
        'activate_url': 'https://test.zulip.org',
        'support_email': 'admin@zulip.org',
        'zulip_support': 'admin@zulip.org',
        'unsubscribe_link': 'https://unsub.zulip.org',
    }

    # Do not render these templates,
    # as they are currently unsupported
    ignore = [
        'digest',
        'missed_message',
        'password_reset',
    ]

    files = os.listdir(os.path.join(ZULIP_PATH, 'templates', 'zerver', 'emails'))
    templates = []  # type: List[str]
    data = []

    for f in files:
        template = f.split('.')[0]
        if template not in templates and template not in ignore:
            templates.append(template)
            try:
                data.append(render_email(template, test_context))
            except Exception as e:
                print('rip')
    return render(request, 'zerver/test_emails.html', {'emails': data})

def render_email(template_prefix, context):
    # type: (str, dict) -> Dict
    email = {} # type: Dict[str, Any]
    email['template'] = template_prefix
    email['subject'] = loader.render_to_string('zerver/emails/' + template_prefix + '.subject', context).strip()
    message = loader.render_to_string('zerver/emails/' + template_prefix + '.txt', context)

    try:
        html_message = loader.render_to_string('/zerver/emails/' + template_prefix + '.html', context)
    except TemplateDoesNotExist:
        html_message = None

    if html_message is not None:
        email['body'] = html_message
        email['text'] = False
    else:
        email['body'] = message
        email['text'] = True

    return email

```

* Use only back-end  and use ScheduledJob to control the when messages are send.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-06-11 20:41 UTC

To set the stage a bit, there are two places where onboarding info is given currently:
1. Messages sent to public streams, when the realm is created, time-delayed on the order of minutes.
2. The tutorial, where you click next a bunch of times 

There are two places where we plan on giving onboarding info in the future: 
A. Messages sent to public (private) streams, when the realm (user) is created, possibly time-delayed
B. A hotspots system for web, maybe something else for mobile. 

B will be client-specific, and have no permanent effect on any non-onboarding part of the product. 1 and A are real messages. 

Currently, 1 is implemented from the frontend, in order to do a time-delay (i.e. first one message shows up, then another one a minute later, etc). My concern with that is e.g. what if someone goes through the onboarding on mobile, or some other client; then their realm is missing out on these beginning messages entirely. Also, I'm not sure how to make a frontend-only implementation robust to e.g. quitting the zulip window 30 seconds after creating a realm. 

So my thought is to do it all on the backend. As a V1, have no time-delay, and just create the messages in do_create_realm and do_create_user. As a V2 .. something, maybe a ScheduledMessage table, or a bot that handles the timing, or something else. I'm mainly just wondering if there's something we're missing about the benefits of 1, and if eventually we will indeed want A to be done in the same way 1 is.

**Aditya Bansal** · 2017-06-20 14:56 UTC

So string in python 3 are by default `unicode` strings which are stored in form of unicode code points in memory.
that is not true in python 2. Python 2 stores strings in form of `bytes` in memory. Here `bytes` literally means bytes or in other words the memory representation of the code points. 
This is the most frustrating problem/difference/backward incompatible behaviour which was necessary to be introduced to newer versions of python.

So what happens is functions in python 3 emit unicode strings where as in python 2 functions spit out `bytes` str.
These are mutually incompatible and we need to convert from one to other.
So encoding is the process of converting or representing code points from unicode representation to bytes representation.
Decoding is its opposite.

**Aditya Bansal** · 2017-06-20 15:18 UTC

```py
def force_bytes(s, encoding='utf-8'):
    # type: (Union[Text, binary_type], str) -> binary_type
    """converts a string to binary string"""
    if isinstance(s, binary_type):
        return s
    elif isinstance(s, Text):
        return s.encode(encoding)
    else:
        raise TypeError("force_bytes expects a string type")
```

## indenting template tags

*2017-06-27 to 2017-06-27 · 12 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/49-development-help/topic/indenting.20template.20tags/with/238601)*

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-06-27 18:55 UTC

Do we indent in the following situation?
```
{% block myblock %}
should this be indented?
{% endblock %}
```
I see both in our codebase.
(My personal vote is no indent, but not enough to rock the boat if we already do it another way.)

**James Rowan** · 2017-06-27 18:59 UTC

The travis build failed for me and told me the indentation was expected when I didn't indent in that situation (hence the whitespace changes in #5547)

**Aditya Bansal** · 2017-06-27 19:05 UTC

It depends upon situation. @Rishi Gupta 
As far as I remember the linter is designed in such a way to have this accepted:
* If we have Jinja2 temp tags, with content inside we should not generally indent for just textual stuff.
* If the jinja2 tag becomes nested with another jinja2 tag we indent the outter one and apply every rule from first on inner one.
* If a jinja2 tag has any html tag inside its body (which are always indented) we indent the jinja2 tag.

Essentially what you can take away from this is if a jinja2 tag is a terminal tag in a nested structure then its body doesn't get an indent.

**Aditya Bansal** · 2017-06-27 19:07 UTC

ping me if you see any behaviour which doesn't match, I will try to either explain it if it was expected or otherwise it might probably a bug.

## settings migrations

*2017-06-28 to 2017-06-28 · 10 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/49-development-help/topic/settings.20migrations/with/238910)*

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-06-28 04:41 UTC

We currently have the following setting in prod_settings_template.py:
`NOREPLY_EMAIL_ADDRESS = 'Zulip <noreply@example.com>'`

We want to change that setting to use the following format instead:
`NOREPLY_EMAIL_ADDRESS = 'noreply@example.com'`

What is the best way to do this? Some ideas:
* If we could run some code after `/etc/settings` is loaded, we could force whatever the user puts into the format that we want. 
* Write a script that changes everyone's prod settings file on upgrade (though then it's slightly broken if they downgrade). 
* Force the setting into the format we want every time we import the setting.

Thoughts on the best way to proceed? @James Rowan fyi

**James Rowan** · 2017-06-28 16:08 UTC

One advantage to the last option of "defensive `email.utils.parseaddr`s" is that in situations where we don't want to change the sender name, whatever the user supplies could be used.  This might be handy for e.g. invitation emails, where having it come  from "Acme Corp Zulip <noreply@acme.com>" rather than "Zulip <noreply@acme.com>" may even be better.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-28 16:23 UTC

I'm strongly in favor of just having a defensive/versatile way of dealing with mutiple formats:
* It's easier to make it backward compatible.
* Doing things at upgrade time is really hard to test from a manual perspective.
* Doing stuff at import time is less than ideal for making code testable.
* If I understand James's point correctly, he's saying that the long format can sometimes still be nice, which I agree with.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-06-28 17:34 UTC

One disadvantage of option 3 is that whenever a future developer wants to use this setting, they'll need to correctly know about and deal with the versatility. And if they don't, it's a pretty subtle bug.

Regarding the last point, I think it doesn't make sense to have a mix of using the user's long format and just their address. We're currently taking control of the display name 90% of the time, so I think it's more straightforward to just do it 100% of the time. And if we do ever have a customizable sender, it would be a realm setting, not a server setting.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-28 17:49 UTC

I don't really share your concerns about future developers using the setting, because it's pretty easy to encapsulate the transformation in a function and put tests around it.

But your points about us doing it 90% of the time already do resonate with me.

I don't think there's any perfect solution here, because the upgrade path is gonna be tricky here, and doing it at import feels dev-unfriendly to me.  I can elaborate on why I think import is a bad idea if you are leaning that way.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-06-28 18:08 UTC

oh, maybe I misunderstood which solution you were suggesting. Are you suggesting "If we could run some code after /etc/settings is loaded, we could force whatever the user puts into the format that we want."? (If so, I also think that is best, if there is a way to do it)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-28 18:15 UTC

In some sense of "after", I am suggesting we run code after settings is loaded that forces whatever the user puts into settings into the format that we want.  But I'm not sure it's exactly what you meant, so let me just say what I'd do:

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-28 18:17 UTC

* Change all of our places in the code that directly use the setting to instead use a helper function to get the reply address.
* Write a lint rule that basically prevents any new code from directly using the setting.
* Change our helper function to deal with both the old format and the new format.

I think this is the most robust solution for the short term.  In parallel, we can start a deprecation process, where we do things like instruct people how to change the setting to a simpler value, etc.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-06-28 18:53 UTC

ah, got it. I like this solution and have an idea for how to do it; @James Rowan let me quickly throw this together and then you can build on top of it.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-06-28 20:16 UTC

put some pseudocode up at https://github.com/rishig/zulip/tree/settings-email-post
The first 5 commits should be merged as a part of #5607. The next commit I realized should just be a part of the main "change from_email to (from_name, from_address)" commit. And then something like the last commit can come at the end. 

I think this is also clear enough that we won't need a lint rule (lint rules that check the whole codebase carry some perf cost, I think).

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-06 20:12 UTC

The story's actually slightly more complicated.  The tool is called `./tools/check-templates`.  The original version checked for opening and closing tags matching up, plus basic html/jinja parse-ability.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-06 20:13 UTC

And then we started migrating templates to all use 4-space indents, and the mechanism there is `pretty_print`, where we `pretty_print` the code to have 4-space indentations.  And then we turn that into a linter by saying you fail lint if pretty_print(file_contents) != file_contents.

**Aditya Bansal** · 2017-07-06 20:18 UTC

one thing I like to point out here is this, whenever `./tools/check-templates` discovers non-proper lint in a file it errors out with the properly formated file which it expects spitted out here `/var/tmp/pretty_html.txt`. So one can use that as a kind of checkup and do even basic linting.
Note: It's not perfect.

## mypy: str vs Text

*2017-07-08 to 2017-07-11 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/49-development-help/topic/mypy.3A.20str.20vs.20Text/with/246077)*

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2017-07-08 03:20 UTC

I've read the zulip mypy doc; while I undestand Text is generally preferred, is it intended that str is retained for file system data?

This was inspired by looking at type checking just within something as simple as tools/check-css.

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2017-07-08 03:28 UTC

(equally, that u is used for FS literals?)

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-08 03:50 UTC

We sorta want to follow Python's conventions, and it might be the case that file access is done via `str` in both Python versions.

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2017-07-08 04:11 UTC

Some provisional reading suggested looking at sys.getfilesystemencoding (os.fsencode/fsdecode in python 3 help?). Presumably with international users then the filesystem could be encoded differently and be relevant for zulip config paths? (yes, not relevant to tools, I assume at least)

In this case I changed Text to str and mypy no longer complains (with py2 and py3), but I wasn't sure if this was simply a 'fix' around a larger problem.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-08 04:17 UTC

Don't have time to dig into that right now; I'm not sure what the situation is.  But I think we should probably assume that the Zulip server has a controlled locale, since we can set the locale for the server if we need to.

**Greg Price** · 2017-07-11 22:00 UTC

@Neil Pilgrim Catching up on this as I'm back online today :)

`Text` [is defined as](http://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/latest/kinds_of_types.html#text-and-anystr) just an alias of the Unicode-string type in both Python 2 and Python 3 -- so `unicode` and `str` respectively. So the difference between `Text` and `str` is only in what they mean in Python 2.

**Greg Price** · 2017-07-11 22:03 UTC

In Python 2, what a lot of filesystem methods do is try to follow your lead -- if you pass them `str` filenames, they return `str`, and if you pass `unicode` they return `unicode`. E.g., [os.listdir](https://docs.python.org/2/library/os.html#os.listdir):
> On Windows NT/2k/XP and Unix, if path is a Unicode object, the result will be a list of Unicode objects.

**Greg Price** · 2017-07-11 22:05 UTC

In our code we're going to generally be building paths with plain string literals -- it'd be unusual to write something like `u'/var/log/zulip'`, with the `u`. So that means we get `str` paths. On Python 2, the stdlib follows our lead and gives us `str` paths back.

**Greg Price** · 2017-07-11 22:09 UTC

On Python 3, the story from the stdlib is differently complicated, with the concept of [path-like objects](https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-path-like-object). But in particular, if we always provide `str` objects, we get `str` objects back. So I think that's what we want to do.

**Greg Price** · 2017-07-11 22:24 UTC

The one big would-be wrinkle I see in that plan is that on a Linux system -- like a Zulip server -- paths at the system level are actually byte strings, and may not be valid UTF-8. Fortunately, Python 3 has a solution to that! Since [PEP 383](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0383/) in Python 3.1, pathnames that don't decode cleanly have been converted losslessly from invalid UTF-8 (or whatever) to invalid Unicode strings, in a round-trip-lossless way.

**Greg Price** · 2017-07-11 22:26 UTC

So the only small wrinkle, I think, is that we should make sure the Zulip server system has a consistent encoding in its locale, namely UTF-8. In practice I think it's unlikely a server someone tries to set up Zulip on will have any other encoding configured, so I'm inclined to defer worrying about that until we hear from someone actually having trouble.

## confirmation links in hex?

*2017-07-09 to 2017-07-12 · 16 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/49-development-help/topic/confirmation.20links.20in.20hex.3F/with/246624)*

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-07-09 04:36 UTC

All our confirmation links are in hex (meaning, they use [0-9a-f]). Any reason for not using [0-9a-zA-Z]? It would shorten the keys from 40 characters to 28 or so, so not a huge deal, but curious if there's some benefit to the restriction.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-09 11:05 UTC

I think using all the letters to get a shorter key is a good plan.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-09 15:41 UTC

Yeah, we can do that if we think it'll look nicer.  `random_api_key` in `zerver/lib/create_user.py` uses a base-64 encoding based algorithm for this purpose.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-07-09 17:27 UTC

Currently we're using 192 bit keys (32 characters), e.g. `bl0yJJhiLOrpNvNOxEs4mhtQrs7mViU0`. If we're fine with 128 bit keys that would drop it to 21 characters, and if we're fine with 80 bit keys it would drop it to 14 characters.
The only attacks I can think of are 
* Someone brute force trying a bunch of confirmation links, by going to `zulip.acme.com/accounts/register/<confirmation link>`. A trillion requests/second * 10 years gives something like 65 bits.
* `os.urandom` dropping to a prng in some installations, and then using that fact to reduce the search space. Not sure how much buffer to afford to this.

Thoughts? Am I missing something? I think in crypto key lengths are longer, because the key breaker gets a lot of hints (e.g. maybe they get to see some text + that text encrypted with the key).

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-09 17:34 UTC

I think we're ok here.  A more compressed encoding is no less secure than an overly verbose encoding that only uses 16 characters.  And from a general security perspective, I think we're ok.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-09 18:46 UTC

Yeah, the big concern here that might cause one to want to use an excessive number of bits is issues with a weak random number generator.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-07-09 19:31 UTC

hmm. 192 still seems a bit excessive. How would you feel about 96 (or just under, given how we create these)? 96 would give 30+ bits of margin, assuming a trillion requests/second * a few weeks (I realized the links expire in a day, so 10 years doesn't help the attacker).

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-09 19:51 UTC

I think we need to do some research into what one can rely on with prngs before making a change here.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-07-09 20:46 UTC

My understanding of this is we only care about `/dev/urandom` on linux? Based on too much time spent reading I'm basically happy to treat that as pure randomness (after the initial startup). Mathematically speaking, breaking `dev/urandom` seems no easier than breaking e.g. 256-bit SSL. E.g. an extremely conservative model of what's going on in `/dev/urandom` is that we start with 256 bits of true randomness, and then generate a string of bits using that true randomness.
(Conservative, because in practice, those 256 bits are being refreshed constantly.)

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-07-09 21:43 UTC

^^^ Thoughts on this, @Archana?

**Greg Price** · 2017-07-11 22:33 UTC

I agree with that model of `/dev/urandom` (except the number in my head was that it targets 128 bits before it considers itself properly started up, not 256, but I haven't checked that.)

**Greg Price** · 2017-07-11 22:37 UTC

The main case where `/dev/urandom` is not practically equivalent to a stream of random bytes is where the system is in some kind of environment where the kernel `random` driver really isn't able to get much entropy. That can happen on some seriously underpowered devices -- e.g. it's been known to happen on cheap consumer routers. I believe it's also been known to happen on VMs in some clouds, though I don't see a technical reason that *should* be the case -- the hypervisor should be able to provide the VM with a solid seed from its own `/dev/urandom` or equivalent.

**Greg Price** · 2017-07-11 22:37 UTC

I don't think in those cases we'd really gain anything by drawing more bits from the stream, though -- the issue there is that the entire stream doesn't contain much entropy.

**Alex Dehnert** · 2017-07-12 23:45 UTC

> I believe it's also been known to happen on VMs in some clouds, though I don't see a technical reason that should be the case -- the hypervisor should be able to provide the VM with a solid seed from its own /dev/urandom or equivalent.

For my local VMs, my recollection is that it took a bit of effort to figure out how to make that work (at least a couple years ago), and I think it might have involved something in the VM. It's possible that it's just "some clouds haven't gotten their act together enough to set up feeding entropy into their VMs, on the host and/or default image setup". (I have vague memories that Linux now has a paravirt entropy driver or something?)

**Greg Price** · 2017-07-12 23:47 UTC

Yeah, probably I should have said I don't see a *fundamental* technical reason. I don't know the specifics of existing APIs for that, but it wouldn't surprise me at all if e.g. Linux currently makes this a pain to make happen.

**Greg Price** · 2017-07-12 23:48 UTC

Or if Linux or some other common guest or hypervisor doesn't support it at all.

## sockets in dev

*2017-07-15 to 2017-07-19 · 27 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/49-development-help/topic/sockets.20in.20dev/with/251055)*

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-15 00:55 UTC

I'm seeing this in certain situations in dev:

~~~
web app -> 100% -> socket code -> 100% -> tornado queue -> 100% 
-> server -> 100% -> tornado -> 1 / N -> socket code
~~~

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-15 00:57 UTC

The overall symptom is that only 1 out of N messages gets acked by the server, even though the server is handling the requests (and sending events back successfully too).

The pattern is always very round robin.  One request will fully round trip, then N-1 don't, then one does, etc.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-15 02:54 UTC

@Tim Abbott @Greg Price @Umair Khan I figured out what's happening here, at least on a high level:

* when you start run-dev.py using WEBSOCKETS=True (the default value), 100% of your server requests get acked back to the client via the `tornado_return` message
* if you change Python code, the server automatically restarts, and now you get 50% of server requests acked
* each subsequent restart lowers your ack ratio: 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5, 1/6, etc.

What I'm not sure of is the exact mechanism.  I assume some client of the `tornado_return` queue is getting zombied in some way that it's still part of some round robining scheme, but it's actually dead.  I'm not sure on that.

Help would be appreciated.  I think this is a pretty serious problem for our dev environment, because the failures are kind of subtle in our app, since a lot of things mostly still work via the events.

**Greg Price** · 2017-07-15 02:55 UTC

Huh, fascinating.

**Greg Price** · 2017-07-15 02:56 UTC

Definitely agree this is a priority. I'm going afk shortly for the weekend, but if you or someone else online doesn't diagnose it tonight, this would be good to file as an issue to help us make sure we follow up.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-15 02:57 UTC

It took me a few hours to debug it.  I'm calling it quits for the night.  The tricky thing for me now is that consumers wrap each other, so when I try to find places to put print statements, I am now landed on the UserActivityWorker instead of the `tornado_return` worker.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-15 02:59 UTC

The workaround is to set USE_WEBSOCKETS to False.  This isn't urgent for the weekend, but I suspect Tim will chime in pretty soon if there is some obvious thing here we need to fix.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-15 03:00 UTC

https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/5809 was my reproducer.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-15 21:05 UTC

@Steve Howell So, an important detail that may be relevant to this problem is that we run queue workers multithreaded in development.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-15 21:06 UTC

So, the issue you were seeing with `UserActivityWorker` could be related to that?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-15 21:06 UTC

Though I don't understand what you mean by "consumers wrap each other"

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-15 22:36 UTC

This function shows in the traceback when the payload is sent, but the `callback` points to an activity worker:

~~~

**Umair Khan** · 2017-07-17 04:07 UTC

Will try this today.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-17 18:10 UTC

Any findings from debugging this @Umair Khan?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-17 18:32 UTC

I created #5824.  I'll flesh this out if we get stuck.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-07-18 03:57 UTC

@Tim Abbott, nope. I ended working on i18next caching thing. Doing this now.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-07-18 05:34 UTC

So I think the problem is that our Tornado server doesn't restart when Django restarts.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-07-18 05:37 UTC

I ran the Torando server separately, forced a restart of Django by changing the code, tested with `compose.test()` and it failed as expected, then I restarted the Tornado server, without restarting either `run-dev` or Django server, and everything worked correctly.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-07-18 05:39 UTC

Probably the simplest solution is to restart `runtornado` whenever Django restarts.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-07-18 05:57 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-18 06:10 UTC

Interesting!

**Umair Khan** · 2017-07-18 06:12 UTC

I think the Tornado restarts through Tornado's autoreload but the process id remains same.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-07-18 06:12 UTC

So I think the file descriptors are not garbage collected, perhaps?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-18 07:02 UTC

Oh, interesting, that seems like a plausible explanation.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-07-18 08:02 UTC

>What I'm not sure of is the exact mechanism. I assume some client of the tornado_return queue is getting zombied in some way that it's still part of some round robining scheme, but it's actually dead. I'm not sure on that.

Yeah, `runtornado` manages one queue.  On every restart this queue instead of getting cleaned up becomes a zombie. So after one restart we have one zombie queue and we lose one message, after two restarts we have two zombie queues and we lose two messages and so.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-18 08:55 UTC

Thanks @Umair Khan for looking into this!

**Umair Khan** · 2017-07-19 05:51 UTC

It turns out that we were not closing the connection to the queue on Tornado reload. Fixed in #5857.

**Vishnu KS** · 2017-07-19 21:55 UTC

For facilitating this I added recipeint_realm as an argument to `recipient_for_emails`. This was necessary because the realm of the sender and the realm of the receivers can be different when cross realm bot is sending the message. The  last 3 commits in #5867 tackles this. ```python
 with assert_disallowed():
            self.send_message(feedback_email, [user1_email, user2_email],
                              Recipient.PERSONAL)

```
The test is making feedback_bot to send PM to 2 users on different realms. This was fine earlier because we didn't need realm information for accessing user_profiles . The `recipient_for_emails` functions's recipeint_realm argument ws added expecting that all the receivers have the same realm.  Should I update `recipient_for_emails` so that it works with recipients from multiple realms (pass a list of realms maybe) just to make the tests work?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-19 22:01 UTC

Do `ZulipTestCase.send_message`and `check_send_message` still support passing in multiple emails?   If so, I think the test is legitimate, and we just need to make sure there's something "inside" of `check_send_message` that will satisy the `assert_disallowed()` assertion.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-19 22:02 UTC

(but we could be moving the error handling out of `recipient_for_emails` and up to a higher place in the call stack, if that makes any sense)

**Vishnu KS** · 2017-07-19 22:55 UTC

I think I can do validation without passing the realm to recipient_for_emails. Let me see if that works :)

**Vishnu KS** · 2017-07-19 23:12 UTC

Looks like it is not possible to do that without the recipients realm. When the sender is a cross realm bot we don't have realm information of  recipients  to obtain the user profiles.

**Vishnu KS** · 2017-07-19 23:15 UTC

I will add recipents_realm as an argument to recipient_for_emails and use UserProfile.DoesNotExist validation error for assert_disallowed.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-19 23:20 UTC

At first glance it appears to me that you don't need to pass in a realm to `recipient_for_emails`, and you can just infer the primary realm from `sender` and then use that for all normal users (and complain if their lookup fails).  And then for the cross-realm-bots, just exempt them from the validation according to the current logic.  And look up their ids using a special cross-bot-specific lookup function.

**Vishnu KS** · 2017-07-19 23:22 UTC

If the sender is cross realm bot and the recipients are normal users we would be needing realm information right for accessing their userprofiles?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-19 23:23 UTC

Oh, huh, that's an ugly edge case.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-19 23:25 UTC

The cross-bot realms are all under our control.  So it's possible that we should first do a refactoring where cross-realm-bot bots always specify user_ids of sendees, not emails.  And then the cross-realm bots can bypass some of the lookup-by-email-and-realm checks, since it's all internal.  I'm thinking out loud here--I don't know how easy that would be to do.  But I would consider taking on that pre-refactoring, even if it's not super easy, as I ultimately think our internal code to send internal message should all be userid-based, not email-based.

**Vishnu KS** · 2017-07-19 23:31 UTC

Okay. That makes sense. Do you think it makes sense for now to just pas the realm of all the recipients as an extra argument. It should be a single realm right as we don't have any cases in which we are PMing users in multiple realms at the same time(except in tests).

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-19 23:36 UTC

Technically, due to the somewhat hacky way that cross-realm bots work now, it's possible to send PMs to users who belong to multiple realms.  It's not possible, as far as I remember, to PM multiple "normal" users who belong to different realms, but it is possible to PM a normal user and a cross-realm user.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-19 23:44 UTC

I am trying to think of the worse case scenario.  Let's say we have a cross-realm bot called the "help bot" that responds to user PMs with help text.  Imagine this setup
* help-bot lives on the special realm 0
* vishnu@example.com has accounts on realms 4, 7, and 9
* vishnu@example.com, while logged on to realm 7, sends help-bot a message asking for help
* our code triggers help-bot to respond to @vishnu@example.com on realm 7
* vishnu on realm 7 responds to help-bot and copies steve@example.com (also on realm 7)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-19 23:45 UTC

I think all of this should be legal, and we should have test coverage to prove it gets through.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-19 23:46 UTC

But we should continue to make it illegal for vishnu@example.com#realm-4 to send a message to vishnu@example.com-7.  And it should **definitely** be illegal (and tested) that vishnu@example.com#realm-4 can't send to tim@example.com#realm-8.

**Vishnu KS** · 2017-07-19 23:51 UTC

> vishnu on realm 7 responds to help-bot and copies steve@example.com (also on realm 7)

I didn't knew this scenario was possible. Thanks for giving a solid example :)

**Vishnu KS** · 2017-07-19 23:59 UTC

Let me see what I can do with cross realm bots specifying user ids always. That is definitely a much cleaner solution to this problem I think.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-20 00:02 UTC

The other concrete example to dwell on is this:

* help-bot sends a message to vishnu@example.com, who lives on multiple realms, but only the only **intended** recipient is (user_id=5682, realm_id=5, email=vishnu@example.com)

I think for that case, we possibly want to have two separate code paths.  If the cross-realm bot is the sender, want to avoid "email" at the earliest place possible in the code stack, even if that requires us to split up some of existing functions to have ways to send user_ids all the way through the code stack for some cases, but deal more with emails and implicit realms in other code paths.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-20 00:05 UTC

I think a lot of the initial refactorings will be like this:

Existing code:

~~~ python
def foo_on_email(email):
     # all the guts
~~~

New code:

~~~ python
def foo_on_email(email)
    user_id = appropriate_lookup_function(email)
    foo_on_user_id(user_id)

def foo_on_user_id(user_id)
    # all the guts
~~~

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-20 00:14 UTC

And to make it more concrete:

validate_recipient_user_ids: does all the heavy lifting on who can talk to who, but doesn't have to figure out user ids (and cross-realm-bot senders can call this directly)

validate_recipient_emails(emails, sender_user_id): delegates most things to validate_recipient_ids, but knows how to map email -> user_id using the implicit realm of sender_user_id and not caring about realm for cross-realm-bot emails

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-20 18:07 UTC

Yeah, that user ID approach is probably good for a lot of these potentially cross-realm cases.

## mypy update feedback

*2017-08-04 to 2017-08-04 · 3 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/49-development-help/topic/mypy.20update.20feedback/with/262707)*

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2017-08-04 04:06 UTC

After working on some general mypy updates with the latest mypy, @Tim Abbott suggested upgrading the version installed by zulip to 0.521, which is the latest release; my work on this is ongoing in #6014. This exposes some new issues combined with typing/mypy, which I thought would be good to discuss here before committing, or raising them upstream; they are visible in the original travis build failure (https://travis-ci.org/zulip/zulip/jobs/260776561) and each has an associated commit (except parts 4,6, 7):

1. `zerver/lib/contextmanagers.py`: after discussion online, the `flock` contextmanager probably needs to take an `IO[Any]` rather than an `int`, though that won't work with python2. Therefore in #6014 a commit sets this to `Any`.
2. `tools/linter_lib/custom_check.py`: the issue here is that the `RuleList`type alias is within `build_custom_checkers()`, which apparently now doesn't pass mypy.  Is this a mypy regression or correct? I've set it to just be outside the function in #6014.
3. `zerver/tests/test_*`: `tornado_redirected_to_list` in `zerver/lib/test_helpers.py` expects a List[Mapping], but quite a few calls use List[Dict]; the former wasn't changed recently, so I expect this was either a mypy bug or the change in types crept in recently? Commit in #6104.
4. `zerver/tests/test_[decorators|messages].py`: the issue here appears to be with the `Request` objects having members added? I'm unsure how to resolve all these cases; I'm hoping someone familiar with the code (REQ pattern?) can shed some light. :star:
5. `zerver/lib/test_helpers.py`: the parameter to `simulated_queue_client` was set to `type`, which (unsurprisingly?) caused a problem; my commit in #6104 changes this to a minimal `Callable`.
6. `zerver/lib/test_helpers.py`: unicode<->str issue, only in python2; no commit yet. :star:
7. `tools/print-all/print-all`: TextIO/BinaryIO issue, only in python3 (probably unicode issue too?); no commit yet. :star:

Any thoughts, particularly on :star:s, gratefully received :simple_smile:

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-08-04 17:36 UTC

@Neil Pilgrim for 1, I'd use a `type: ignore # https://github.com/link/to/typeshed/issue`.  That's our standrd strategy for marking mypy bugs that will result in us fixing the annotation again once the bug is fixed.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-08-04 17:38 UTC

4. For `test_decorators.py`, if it's the validator tests, the whole point of most of those tests in question is to make sure sending the wrong thing throws the right error, so those may be tricky.  Might want to just use `type: ignore`.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-03-16 09:32 UTC

There are also unofficial conventions when writing automated tests:
- Use Iago for admin-related tests.
- Use Polonius for guest-related tests.
- Use Cordelia and Hamlet as the "normal" users.
- Use Othello as the "other" user, such as the user who gets **excluded** from a result when you're trying to test that a function doesn't return too many values.  (Note that OTHEllo and OTHEr start with the same four letters)

**Steve Howell** · 2021-03-16 09:33 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-16 16:16 UTC

https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/subsystems/html-css.html covers various things but not `opts`, which is just a naming convention for a dictionary/object passed into a function.  Long-term, I expect many but not all of those will be replaced with nicer syntax once we move to TypeScript.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-04-16 16:34 UTC

We can clean a lot of that up in es6, actually.  (And we have already in various places.)

**Steve Howell** · 2021-04-16 16:36 UTC

Any code like this:

~~~ js
function foo(opts) {
   fred(opts.a, opts.b);
   // don't pass opts as a whole thing to anything else
}
~~~

can be transformed like so:

~~~ js
function foo({a, b}) {
    fred(a, b)
}
~~~

def accounts_home_with_realm_str(request, realm_str):
    # type: (HttpRequest, str) -> HttpResponse
    if not settings.REALMS_HAVE_SUBDOMAINS and completely_open(get_realm(realm_str)):
        # You can sign up for a completely open realm through a
        # special registration path that contains the domain in the
        # URL. We store this information in the session rather than
        # elsewhere because we don't have control over URL or form
        # data for folks registering through OpenID.
        request.session["realm_str"] = realm_str
        return accounts_home(request)

def completely_open(realm):

    # This realm is completely open to everyone on the internet to
    # join. E-mail addresses do not need to match a realmdomain and
    # an invite from an existing user is not required.
    if not realm:
        return False
    return not realm.invite_required and not realm.restricted_to_domain

## PYTHONWARNINGS=ignore: command not found

*2017-08-16 to 2017-08-16 · 18 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/49-development-help/topic/PYTHONWARNINGS.3Dignore.3A.20command.20not.20found/with/269106)*

**Vishnu KS** · 2017-08-16 18:50 UTC

I am getting the following error in master while running `test-all`
```shell
----
Running ./tools/lint --pep8

----
Running ./manage.py makemessages --locale en
processing locale en
[frontend] processing locale en

----
Running PYTHONWARNINGS=ignore ./tools/check-capitalization --no-generate
./tools/test-all: line 25: PYTHONWARNINGS=ignore: command not found
```

**Vishnu KS** · 2017-08-16 18:50 UTC

I am getting this in both my local env and remote vm.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-08-16 18:55 UTC

Ahh, that's a bug; I'll fix it shortly.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-08-16 18:57 UTC

Merged debfe708d02887970724cab38ca79768c9a41c6f, thanks for the report!  @Greg Price FYI

**Greg Price** · 2017-08-16 19:14 UTC

Ah indeed, thanks!

**Greg Price** · 2017-08-16 19:18 UTC

This is kind of a funny shell wrinkle -- the issue is that when you get a command as a shell array and try to run it like this:
```
"$@"
```
apparently that doesn't interpret the `VAR=val VAR2=val2 ...` syntax for setting environment variables.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-08-16 19:23 UTC

Yeah.  It makes sense if you think about how that syntax works

**Greg Price** · 2017-08-16 19:25 UTC

Yeah, it's certainly understandable, though I think the other way would've been equally understandable.

**Greg Price** · 2017-08-16 19:26 UTC

Basically a matter of what happens first in the long sequence of things the shell does to interpret a command.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-08-16 19:34 UTC

I think in this case, the alternative wouldn't really make sense, since from the shell's perspective, the `PYTHONWARNINGS=` part could just be argparse-style arguments to `run`.

**Greg Price** · 2017-08-16 20:25 UTC

Nono, this isn't about the `run` command. Those obviously become arguments to `run`.

**Greg Price** · 2017-08-16 20:25 UTC

But what `run` does is then run its arguments as a command.

**Greg Price** · 2017-08-16 20:25 UTC

```
function run {
    echo '----'
    echo "Running $@"
    if ! "$@"; then
```

**Greg Price** · 2017-08-16 20:27 UTC

Specifically, the `"$@"`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-08-16 20:28 UTC

Ahh, I see, and you were hoping that would work

**Greg Price** · 2017-08-16 20:28 UTC

It turns out that when the command described by those arguments begins with some items that look like `VAR=value`, they don't get interpreted as assignments to the environment and instead get interpreted as the command program and its first arguments.

**Greg Price** · 2017-08-16 20:29 UTC

Right -- well, I wasn't thinking this specifically about it or I would have tried it :), but implicitly I saw the helper `run` which runs its arguments as a command and I just rewrote that command the same way I was rewriting the command elsewhere.

**Greg Price** · 2017-08-16 20:30 UTC

But it turns out that a shell function that calls `"$@"` runs its arguments "as a command" in a less-interpreted, later-stage sense than I'd implicitly assumed.

**Shane Kearns** · 2017-08-17 21:01 UTC

I'd probably just do a filename convention unless they're dramatically different

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-08-19 01:10 UTC

Struggling to get file upload working, on code that I remember working a few weeks ago. Traceback is below. The error makes me wonder if it has to do with python 2->3, but not sure where unicode issues would come up.
```
In [1]: user = UserProfile.objects.first()

In [2]: user
Out[2]: <UserProfile: AARON@zulip.com <Realm: zulip 1>>

In [3]: from zerver.lib.upload import upload_avatar_image

In [4]: upload_avatar_image(open('static/images/cute/turtle.png'), user, user)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
UnicodeDecodeError                        Traceback (most recent call last)
<ipython-input-4-ca27eb2083d2> in <module>()
----> 1 upload_avatar_image(open('static/images/cute/turtle.png'), user, user)

/srv/zulip/zerver/lib/upload.py in upload_avatar_image(user_file, acting_user_profile, target_user_profile)
    561 def upload_avatar_image(user_file, acting_user_profile, target_user_profile):
    562     # type: (File, UserProfile, UserProfile) -> None
--> 563     upload_backend.upload_avatar_image(user_file, acting_user_profile, target_user_profile)
    564 
    565 def upload_icon_image(user_file, user_profile):

/srv/zulip/zerver/lib/upload.py in upload_avatar_image(self, user_file, acting_user_profile, target_user_profile)
    479         file_path = user_avatar_path(target_user_profile)
    480 
--> 481         image_data = user_file.read()
    482         write_local_file('avatars', file_path + '.original', image_data)
    483 

/srv/zulip-py3-venv/lib/python3.4/codecs.py in decode(self, input, final)
    317         # decode input (taking the buffer into account)
    318         data = self.buffer + input
--> 319         (result, consumed) = self._buffer_decode(data, self.errors, final)
    320         # keep undecoded input until the next call
    321         self.buffer = data[consumed:]

UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0x89 in position 0: invalid start byte
```

**Greg Price** · 2017-08-19 01:35 UTC

Sounds like `user_file` is opened with mode`r` or something, when it should be `rb`.

**Greg Price** · 2017-08-19 01:36 UTC

This is indeed a 2->3 gotcha -- with Python 3, `open` (well, the file object it returns) by default will try to decode the input data with the default encoding, in order to produce `str` data. But for an image, of course, we want bytes.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-08-19 01:41 UTC

cool, that was it!

**Shane Kearns** · 2017-08-25 14:43 UTC

Update: a "privileged" script still connects with ssh and uses sudo; so the `usermod` command can't be used (and directly changing the password file causes an scp error deep in the vagrant internals).
What is possible is to create a "zulip" user inside the box with the matching uid/gid, however you then need to run `sudo -u zulip -i` after `vagrant ssh` in order to run tests as the correct user

Hmm, that's kinda annoying.

**Shane Kearns** · 2017-08-30 14:22 UTC

Another option would be to make the bind-mount read-only, and create a /srv/zulip directory structure inside the container which has symlinks to the correct places; while leaving /srv/zulip/var as a writable directory that exists only inside the container

**Shane Kearns** · 2017-08-30 14:23 UTC

That would prevent creation of `.pyc` files though

## reverse migrations

*2017-09-02 to 2017-09-12 · 18 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/49-development-help/topic/reverse.20migrations/with/276059)*

**Aditya Bansal** · 2017-09-02 17:49 UTC

So I was reading about `sqlmigrate` command on django docs and read about `--backwards` param. Question that arises in my mind is can all migrations be reversed. Like can they be automatically be reversed or after some effort they all can be reversed or something else.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-02 17:56 UTC

A lot of things can be automatically reversed, including almost all of the model-change things that you get from having Django automatically create migrations for you.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-02 17:57 UTC

For migrations that are written by hand, such as the recent migration I wrote to move "muted topics" data from a UserProfile field to a new table, you would have to write a reverse migration by hand, and it's easy to specify.  I chose not to for that one.

**Aditya Bansal** · 2017-09-02 18:01 UTC

hmm, I once saw a issue in our tracker on github relating to making db reverse migrations work for downgrading zulip or something like that. So on a wild observational guess I am going to say the changes that are destructive in nature like deletion of stuff would be very hard to revert. So can they also be always handled?

**Aditya Bansal** · 2017-09-02 18:04 UTC

I guess #280 is the issue.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-02 18:04 UTC

Huh, I don't know what our policy on downgrades is, but I think we should mostly discourage downgrades and focus our energy on making upgrades reliable.  Downgrades open up a whole can of worms besides migrations--they unfix bug fixes, they require downgrading all dependencies, they would have to remove new file artifacts from the upgrade, etc.

**Aditya Bansal** · 2017-09-02 18:06 UTC

yeah, there seems to be lot of nasty things that will be haunting us if we try to support downgrading.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-02 18:11 UTC

I'll use muted topics as a case study.  There are three migrations:
* create new MutedTopic model
* populate MutedTopic from UserProfile.muted_topics (non-reversible)
* drop UserProfile.muted

For testing purposes on this site, we'll only deploy the first two migrations originally, so we can get burn-in.  And we can reverse them and be back right where we want to be, except for mutes users did in the interim.  (So it's essentially a rollback to the user's perspectives.)

After we do the third migration, I think we'll also be able to reverse the 1st and 3rd migration, but that would be more more destructive, since it would have to set muted_topics to its default data, essentially wiping out all of a user's topic mutes.  But the app would still at least work.

**Aditya Bansal** · 2017-09-02 18:15 UTC

so we can't possibly pick up data from `UserProfile.muted_topics`?

**Aditya Bansal** · 2017-09-02 18:15 UTC

i mean `MutedTopic model`

**Aditya Bansal** · 2017-09-02 18:17 UTC

though I get it, if we talk about individual migration's reverse migration that is not necessarily same as what we would want from a series of migrations being reverted.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-02 18:25 UTC

In the case of MutedTopic, it wouldn't be hard to write the reverse conversion, since we have most of the code already written in order to support clients that still want JSON blobs.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-02 18:26 UTC

But it would require some thought, still, as we'd need to combine the 2nd and 3rd migrations so that reversal can be atomic.

**Aditya Bansal** · 2017-09-02 18:28 UTC

yeah, basically at every migration we will need to change granularity level to support such a feature. Also in case of dropping fields completely I guess there is no comeback (Though I guess we never do it)

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-09-02 18:32 UTC

the comeback is to use a default value

**Aditya Bansal** · 2017-09-02 18:35 UTC

hmm, just like seeding value for stuff we don't know :thinking_face:

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-09-12 14:23 UTC

Downgrades is a hard issue.  Given plentiful resources, I'd like to support them, since it can be pretty valuable to be able to downgrade after a new release isn't working.  It should ~always be possible to implement something.  But it's a lot of work to support.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-09-12 14:24 UTC

For muted topics, I think the effect of downgrading is to lose all muted topics, which isn't great, but is better than breaking everything.
